speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). In view of the fact that Victoria day falls on Tuesday this year, will the government consider declaring the Monday nearest May 24 as the legal holiday to be observed generally by the citizens of Canada in this instance?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROPOSAL THAT LEGAL HOLIDAY BE OBSERVED FOR THE PRESENT YEAR ON MONDAY MAY 23
speechtext:
My hon. friend was kind enough to give me an intimation of his intention to ask this question, and I thought it might be of interest to him and to other hon. members of the house if I stated the general position with respect to holidays as provided for in the statutes.
The following are the public statutory holidays in Canada, the dates of which are fixed by statute:
New Year's day Good Friday Easter Monday Victoria day Dominion day Labour day Remembrance day Christmas day.
The following are fixed by proclamation: The sovereign's birthday Thanksgiving day.

Shop Cards Registration
When New Year's day, Christmas day, Victoria day, Dominion day or the sovereign's birthday falls on a Sunday, the following day, in accordance with statutory provision, is observed as the holiday. It will be apparent from this statement that if Victoria day were to be observed on Monday rather than on Tuesday this year, the statute would have to be altered in the meantime. I may say that I have received some communications suggesting that there should be no change, because arrangements have already been made to hold certain celebrations on Tuesday, May 24. I presume once it is understood that the governor in council has no authority in the matter, apart from that given by the statute, it will be apparent that we cannot very well alter the arrangement for Victoria day, at all events for this year.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR REGISTRATION OF DISTINCTIVE

speechtext: Hon. FERNAND RINFRET (Secretary of State) moved the third reading of Bill No. 22, respecting the registration of shop cards by labour unions.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. H. CAHAN (St. Lawrence-St. George):
subtopic: PROVISION FOR REGISTRATION OF DISTINCTIVE
subsubtopic: CARDS OF LABOUR UNIONS AND PREVENTING UNAUTHORIZED USE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I happened to be
called out of the house on April 26 when this bill was in committee. I should now like to make a few remarks with regard to it.
The shop card, which is the subject matter of this legislation, is stated to be desirable in order to afford labour unions, whose members engage not in the production of wares but in the performance of services, means of registering their distinctive cards in order

that those establishments which employ, in the performance of services, members of these unions, may be enabled to use, by arrangement with the unions, the union shop cards and to prevent unauthorized use of the cards.
My only experience with shop cards has been in the barber shop in the city of Montreal, to which I resort occasionally, which displays a card indicating that all the employees of that shop are members of a certain labour union. This is a very proper method of advertising, and I think if it were within our power to do so we might approve of protecting that form of advertising so that a labour union might advertise that in certain shops the employees are all members of its particular union. A similar proposition was made to me some years ago when I was Secretary of State. I investigated the matter in so far as I was able so to do, and the opinion which I reached was at that time clear, and I think, decisive, that it is not within the legislative competence of the parliament of Canada to enact a measure such as this, except possibly by enacting an amendment to the criminal code that would make it a criminal offence for a competitive shop to misuse a card, or to deceive its customers by the display of a card, indicating that its employees were members of a labour union when as a matter of fact they were not such members.	[DOT]
However, when this bill was up for a second reading I asked the Minister of Justice, I think, or the Secretary of State, to have the matter investigated by the Department of Justice, and the Deputy Minister of Justice, for whom I have a great respect indeed, has reported an opinion which appears in Hansard of April 26 last, in which he states that this bill does not deal with trade marks; but he adds, at page 2265:
I am of opinion that the purpose and effect of the bill is to vest in certain labour unions a copyright which they do not now enjoy, and that the validity of the bill is supportable on the ground that it is copyright legislation within the meaning of section 91 (23) of the British North America Act.
As I have already stated, I was clearly of the opinion that this bill or a similar bill was not within the legislative competence of parliament, and that for parliament to enact such legislation beyond its powers would prove a disservice to the labour unions which requested its enactment. I am still of that opinion. I may individually commend the policy of this proposed act, but I think the utmost care should be taken to ensure its

Shop Cards Registration
enactment by a legislature which is constitutionally competent so to do, so that its validity may be beyond doubt.
I am of the opinion that provincial legislatures are competent, and that the bill, if enacted by a provincial legislature, would be valid beyond question.
This bill does not deal with "trade marks." It deals with "shop cards of labour unions." The shop cards are not designs, devices or words to be used to distinguish a manufacturer's or trader's goods, wares or merchandise, and therefore these cards cannot be deemed to be trade marks either at common law or by statute. The bill does not deal with industrial designs, which are defined by our statute law and protected. It is clear, I think, that a shop card is used for advertising purposes only. It advertises, as I have already stated, that the employees of a shop in which a shop card is exhibited are members of a particular labour union.
I remember that when the matter was brought before me as Secretary of State some years ago I spent a great deal of time in examining all the precedents, and I could find no judicial authority to the effect that there may be, by common or statute law, a copyright in such an advertisement.
_ Copyright was originally a common law right which by a series of statutory enactments became merged in the statutory right known as copyright, and since 1911 such statutory right exists in the United Kingdom and in all British dominions and possessions.
Originally, copyright was the exclusive right which an author or designer had, at common law, to print, publish or sell his own original work. Then it was decided by the courts that it included the exclusive right of multiplying copies of an original work. It gave protection also to sculptors, designers and engravers, to authors of literary works, musical compositions, and later, as this house well knows, to performing rights in musical productions. The law of copyright was also extended to protect paintings, drawings and photographs, and works of architecture. But I can find no decision in respect of copyright, either under common law or under the statute law, which purports to protect advertisements.
Chitty, J., in Lamb v. Evans, 1892, 3 Ch. 462, held that there might be copyright in the headings under which advertisements were classified, but not in the advertisements themselves. And in 1893 the court of appeal, 1 Ch. 218, held that though there might not
be copyright in advertisements, there might be copyright in the arrangement of a sheet of advertisements.
Recently it has been found that there is a copyright in the arrangement of statistics in regard to certain branches of insurance, so that those who originated those tables have a copyright in the tables and in their reproduction.
Tradesmen's catalogues may be the subject of copyright, but solely on the ground that the compiler of the catalogue has exercised skill and judgment in making his compilation.
Certainly these shop cards do not fall within that special category of advertisements. This bill does not purport to embody any criminal legislation whatsoever. Ko fines or other penalties are imposed by the bill. It merely provides that a labour union may have a shop card, not on the ground that the labour union is the author of the card, or that it designed the card, but by the mere fact that it has registered a card, as provided in the bill, in a new branch of the state department which is to be organized for that purpose.
Section 9 of the bill provides that a civil action may be brought for unauthorized use of the shop card. I quote:
. 9- t1) An action or suit may be maintained m any court of record having jurisdiction to the amount claimed, by any labour union which has complied with the provisions of this act as to registration, or by any authorized executive officer thereof, against any person, labour union, association, or corporation, alleged to be using without permission the shop card ot such labour union.
That, if passed by a competent legislature, might be commended. But the bill provides merely for a civil action for compensation for the misuse of personal or movable property, and under that provision, in a civil action, damages must be strictly proved. That is' under our English law of torts, an action for deceit. In other words, the bill deals with an alleged deceitful use of property, which is not a trade mark, or a copyright, and is therefore clearly, I think, within the exclusive jurisdiction of the provincial legislatures. The only action that lies under the terms of the bill is an action for compensation for the use or misuse.
Under these circumstances I am personally of the opinion that parliament should hesitate about placing this bill upon the statute books of the country, where it may mislead a number of labour unions, whose work I would highly commend and which should be commended; but they should be protected by a competent legislature, so that they may not be induced to bring actions which, before ultimately
Shop Cards Registration

decided, will involve them in litigation and very considerable expense. I will not now vote against the third reading of the bill, but I thought it was my duty, in view of what has taken place during past years, to express this personal opinion on the third reading.

speechtext:
I hope my hon. friend will not deem it any discourtesy on my part if I do not reply at length to the remarks he has just made. (This bill has been discussed for some time on a previous occasion, when it was up for second reading, and then in committee. On that occasion I had to explain, with my colleague the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers), the reasons why we were bringing it in and recommending it to the attention of the house.
I regret very much to have to disagree with my hon. friend, for whom I have the greatest regard, as also for his legal knowledge; but I must insist that every care was taken in the preparation of this bill, with the aid of officers in both departments, and we are not apprehensive about the point which he has brought up to-day.
I wish merely to remind the house that an amendment to the then Trade Mark and Design Act was adopted on March 25, 1927, to permit the registration of shop cards. That obtained for five years, and never once during that interval has the department been seized of the least doubt as to the validity of such an amendment. In 1932 my hon. friend, who was then secretary of state, brought forward a new bill, the Unfair Competition Act, where he did define "trade mark" in such a way that it would apply only to wares and designs associated with wares, and would not include the registration of shop cards. There is not one word in that bill which does so in a positive way. It was only the effect of the bill, in that as it was dealing only with objects or wares it did exclude automatically the registration of shop cards. But not even when that bill was discussed in the house was there the least allusion made as to whether it was constitutional or not to permit by federal legislation the registration of shop cards.
Since 1932, practically every year, when the labour unions came to Ottawa with a program of desired legislation, the request was made to restore the registration of shop cards. It was pressed before me in 1936 and 1937. I may say that last year we had a bill practically ready to achieve that object, and it was delayed only on account of the short session, which, hon. member's will remember, we had last year.

When I introduced the bill this year, on second reading both the Minister of Labour and myself gave a very full explanation of the trend and the particular character of the measure, and I may add that even since this bill was first discussed there has not been the least intimation to the department, except by my hon. friend the former secretary of state, that it may not be within the jurisdiction of the federal parliament.

After all, Mr. Speaker, a shop card or a design of a labour union is very similar in character to other objects which are protected under several acts of the federal statute. I repeat, Mr. Speaker, that I do not think it is necessary for me to go into the details of

speechtext: This represents a minor amendment consequential upon the former one. The present reading of (j) in the bill means a proposal made 'by a farmer. In view of the change made in the previous sections enabling executors of farmers to make application, the word " farmer " is dropped.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BOARDS OF REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILING PROPOSALS, ETC.
speechtext:
In connection with section 7, it is proposed to drop subsection 3 of section 2 of the present act and substitute what is contained in section 10A of the bill now before the committee. The reason for the change is the wide difference in the opinions of courts and lawyers with reference to the procedure to be adopted by creditors under subsection 3, as it now stands, of section 2 of the act in case of default of a farmer which has been annoying and expensive to all concerned. For that reason it is desired to repeal that subsection and to provide a clear-cut method of dealing with the dishonest farmer, as was intended when the original act was passed, by substituting the new sections 10 and 10A. The real effect of sections 10A and 10A (2) is that whenever a farmer does not carry out the terms of the composition which has been made for him by the board of review, and the reasons for his
not carrying them out are not to be found in circumstances beyond his control, then the remedy provided is that the farmer shall revert to the position occupied by him in relation to his creditor before any order was made by the board.

subtopic: BOARDS OF REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILING PROPOSALS, ETC.
speechtext: Who determines whether the farmer is responsible in the circumstances?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BOARDS OF REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILING PROPOSALS, ETC.
speechtext: The court.

subtopic: BOARDS OF REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILING PROPOSALS, ETC.
speechtext: Is that supposed to be the only remedy? As I understand the decision of the courts at the present time, if someone were supposed to pay a 8100 debt at the rate of S20 a year for five years the creditor could sue, in the ordinary course, for that $20 when it became due. Is it intended now that this provision should be exclusive of other remedies? If a person had a $50 or 8100 debt due him, it should not be necessary for him, before he could sue for that debt, to have the scheme formulated by the board of review annulled. As I understand it, at present one can sue in the ordinary way for a debt due under a proposal that has been confirmed by the board of review, and that is very satisfactory in the case of small debts; it should not be necessary for creditors to have the composition annulled. Is that the idea of the amendment?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BOARDS OF REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILING PROPOSALS, ETC.
speechtext: This amendment provides the remedy set out in it in addition to any other remedies that may exist, particularly those that exist under provincial legislation. This is an additional remedy in the case of a farmer who dishonestly makes no attempt to carry out the terms of the composition that has been made in his favour. It means that under this legislation, in its relationship bo the bankruptcy law, the whole transaction so far as the board of review is concerned is wiped out and the farmer reverts to the position he occupied before any order was made.

subtopic: BOARDS OF REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILING PROPOSALS, ETC.
speechtext:
Since the discussion on March 18, another case has been brought to my attention. A farmer who had already received an order from the board of review before the first payment was due called for an auction sale of his stock and equipment, and the creditors who went to the official receiver to find out what protection they had discovered that they had no remedy under the act. The clause as now drafted is sufficient for the purpose, but it will have to go further. When the matter was under discussion on March 18 I put on Hansard rules 48 and 49, which will be found at page 1494. There are four

Farmers' Creditors Act
reasons for the issuing of an order setting aside a proposal:	They apply where the
debtor has:
(a)	made a fraudulent or preferential conveyance, gift, delivery or transfer of any of his property;	_
(b)	with intent to defeat or delay his creditors, departed or remained out of Canada;
(c)	assigned, removed, secreted or disposed of any of his property with intent to defraud, defeat, or delay his creditors;
(d)	conducted himself to the satisfaction of the official receiver in such manner as indicates bad faith towards his creditors.
The courts have taken the position that the rules apply only prior to the granting of the final order by the board of review. Unless the rules are altered so as to apply to a farmer who has defaulted of his own accord and not in consequence of circumstances, such as climatic conditions, beyond his control; unless it is possible for action to be taken under the rules after the board of review's order is given, then the rules mean nothing. Section 10 (a) as now drafted is satisfactory in that it provides for the cancellation of the order should any of these four reasons be established-and they are serious enough to warrant annulment of the board of review's order. But the rules will have to be altered so as to remove any doubt there may be in the minds of the court that the rules apply after the board of review have made their review as well as before.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BOARDS OF REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILING PROPOSALS, ETC.
speechtext: The matter of amending the rules to make them conform to the intent of the section is now before the department and is under consideration. Of course, the provincial law of contract continues to operate in connection with settlements under this act, and we must be careful not to put in the act anything that might invalidate proceedings because of interference with provincial rights in that regard.

subtopic: BOARDS OF REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILING PROPOSALS, ETC.
speechtext: What will be the position of the farmer if he finds himself unable to carry out the arrangement made prior to the coming into effect of this act? He has been unable to make the payments under the former arrangement; he is in default through no fault of his own. Will he have to have a new proposal formulated, or can he get an extension of time?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BOARDS OF REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILING PROPOSALS, ETC.
speechtext:
He cannot be put into bankruptcy. It is clear that if the farmer is unable to carry out the arrangement through circumstances over which he has no control, this section does not apply. The court would not put that farmer into bankruptcy and thus have him revert to the condition he was in prior to

the issue of the original order of the board of review. As I stated on a former occasion, there is not and cannot be provision for rehearing. If we were to open that subject again I know what would happen. It would be just what has happened on previous occasions; those who wish to have a better deal for the creditors will insist upon some right of appeal from the decisions of the board, from the creditors' point of view. I am afraid that if we provided for appeals or rehearings the value of this legislation would be lost in a tangle of legal proceedings. So it is not proposed to change that part of the statute; there is no intention to create a right of appeal either way. We believe that in that regard the legislation 'has worked as well as can be expected, 'having regard to the difficulties always attendant upon legislation of this kind.

subtopic: BOARDS OF REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILING PROPOSALS, ETC.
speechtext: Do we understand then that it would be within the competence of the board to grant an extension of time without having an appeal made by either creditor or debtor?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BOARDS OF REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILING PROPOSALS, ETC.
speechtext: It is not within the competence of the board, but it is within the competence of the court.

subtopic: BOARDS OF REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILING PROPOSALS, ETC.
speechtext: The farmer would then be considered in default?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BOARDS OF REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILING PROPOSALS, ETC.
speechtext: No, the creditor must go to court to put him in default.

subtopic: BOARDS OF REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILING PROPOSALS, ETC.
speechtext: If the farmer through no fault of his own is unable to meet his obligations, is there no time limit after which the creditor can step in and claim his right? Or will that state of affairs continue indefinitely?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BOARDS OF REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILING PROPOSALS, ETC.
speechtext: It is wholly a matter for the provincial courts, under the law. The creditor can go to court at any time and seek to demonstrate that the farmer is not meeting his obligation although able to do so.

subtopic: BOARDS OF REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILING PROPOSALS, ETC.
speechtext: But in case 'he is not able to do so?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BOARDS OF REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILING PROPOSALS, ETC.
speechtext: That is a matter of adjudication by the judge in each particular case.

subtopic: BOARDS OF REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILING PROPOSALS, ETC.
speechtext: If the judge decides that the farmer is not to blame, and is unable to meet his obligation, can the creditor at no time in the future get the right to press his claim?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BOARDS OF REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILING PROPOSALS, ETC.
speechtext:
In any event, if there were no Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act at all under provincial contract law the creditor

Farmers' Creditors Act
would have to take court proceedings. He is in exactly the same position in that regard with respect to the carrying out of the terms of any order of the board. His position is not changed; the law of contract regulates that.

subtopic: BOARDS OF REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILING PROPOSALS, ETC.
speechtext: One point not to be lost sight of is the avoiding of expense as much as possible. As the wording now stands the first step would be to get an order of the board annulling the composition. That annulment would constitute an act of bankruptcy, and there would then have to be a subsequent application to throw the debtor into bankruptcy-in other words, two separate applications. In the past the practice has been to include both in the one application, for annulment of the composition and the declaration of bankruptcy. As it is worded here there would have to be two separate applications. Has that been considered?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BOARDS OF REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILING PROPOSALS, ETC.
speechtext: It is difficult to get over that situation. In practice I think there would be no second application, because the object of the creditor in most cases would not be to put the farmer into bankruptcy but rather to put him back in the position he occupied in relation to his creditors prior to the order. That could be accomplished on the first application. Creditors generally have not found it to their advantage to put farmers into bankruptcy in the ordinary sense of the term. Only in very rare cases would a second application bringing into effect the ordinary provisions of the Bankruptcy Act be required. But in any case on application to the court the dishonest farmer could be put back into the position he occupied before the board of review made its order.

subtopic: BOARDS OF REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILING PROPOSALS, ETC.
speechtext: I do not think the minister got the point of my first question. If an order is made that someone is to pay a certain sum of money, say $100, in instalments of $20 a year, and the payments are not made, would it be necessary to have the composition annulled before the creditor could sue for the instalments? I take it the minister is under the impression that he would have to have that composition annulled before he could sue.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BOARDS OF REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILING PROPOSALS, ETC.
speechtext: No, I am sorry if I gave that impression. The annulment rests not upon the farmer's inability to pay but upon his honesty in the matter. With respect to the question of suit for the instalments, that is a matter coming under the provincial law of contract, which differs in different provinces. In this legislation we do not interfere with whatever may be the rights of the creditor under provincial law with respect to contracts.

subtopic: BOARDS OF REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILING PROPOSALS, ETC.
speechtext: The minister made a statement as to the law, concerning which I think there may be some question. This act is based upon the insolvency of the farmer. Once he comes under this act on the basis of insolvency, I am inclined to think that the remedies provided by this act are all that are available to the creditor. When a compromise has been effected and an order made providing for payment of instalments over a period of months or years I do not think the creditor can use that order as the basis of an action on contract. It seems to me it must rest for its strength and for any remedies for failure to comply with it upon the provisions found within the four corners of this act; so that if there is default I doubt whether there is an action in the civil court on the terms of the order or compromise. But that is not the objection I rose to point out to the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BOARDS OF REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILING PROPOSALS, ETC.
speechtext: Will my friend permit me to deal with that point first? -because I am under the disadvantage of not being a lawyer although attempting to deal with a complex legal matter.

subtopic: BOARDS OF REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILING PROPOSALS, ETC.
speechtext: The minister is well on the way to becoming a very successful advocate.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BOARDS OF REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILING PROPOSALS, ETC.
speechtext: Thank you. I am advised, with respect to the point now under discussion, that in the various provinces there have been many decisions, all of which, although arriving at the conclusion by different roads, concluded that the order of the board does constitute a new contract and is enforceable under the ordinary law of contract prevailing in the province. Experience has shown that, and the Department of Justice takes the same view. Therefore I think my answer to the hon. member for Rosthern is a correct one, substantiated by legal decisions, that in so far as the order of the board of review is concerned, that order is enforceable in the ordinary way under the law of contract prevailing in the province, because it is held to be a new contract; but that if the creditor deems the debtor dishonest, then under the provisions of the amendment now proposed he may still avail himself of these remedies.

subtopic: BOARDS OF REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILING PROPOSALS, ETC.
speechtext:
As I have said, that is not the point I rose to bring up in connection with this section. I still think it is not a matter of contract; it is an order, and the order stands for what it is worth, which after all I think is very little in most cases.
The objection I wish to urge to this section is in connection with the procedure outlined here. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that it is entirely inconsistent with the procedure that has been laid down in other sections of the act.
Farmers' Creditors Act

Let us see just what is the scheme under this act. A farmer finds himself in financial difficulty, insolvent. He initiates the proceedings; he files a notice and a proposition and all that sort of thing. The proceedings are taken for his benefit and at his instance; an order is made or a compromise is arrived at, which again is for his benefit and to his satisfaction. The hands of the creditors are tied. They cannot move. The farmer goes along and falls into default; he does not carry out his own proposition, or the scheme that has been adopted. Then I submit that the ordinary, regular and fair procedure would be for that farmer to come back to the court and make application for further indulgence, for an extension of time or some modification of the plan, and show that his failure to carry it out has not been his fault. Under this section the procedure is the opposite. The unfortunate creditor whose hands have been tied is the one who must come to the court. He, forsooth, must launch an application; he must take the burden of the proceedings, not because of any default on his part or because of any failure by him to comply with the order of the court. He has to launch these proceedings because somebody else, the farmer, has failed.
Just look at what he has to prove. He goes to the court and makes his application. I do not know just what will be the procedure; I suppose that will be defined in the rules and regulations. Probably he will have to draw up a notice, of motion to serve on the farmer to attend at a certain time and place to show cause why something should not be done against him. Well, the creditor has to go to this expense and take this trouble. He is without knowledge; he is working in the dark. All he knows is that there has been default and that he is not getting what the court ordered him to get. So he has launched these proceedings and served notice on the farmer to come to court. We will say the farmer does not attend the court at all and the judge says, " You have to prove to me that this default is due to something within the control of the farmer." How are you going to prove that? The farmer has not come; he has defaulted again and the judge cannot move because he has no proof. Will he issue a subpoena or summons to bring the farmer to court?

Here you reverse the whole procedure and place upon the creditor the burden of getting what the court has said was his right. You are really putting the cart before the horse. I submit that the whole procedure is wrong; it is contrary to the principles of the act itself and contrary to justice. It is not fair. This section should be redrafted in such.a way that the farmer, who is in default on his own proposition, is the one who must come to the court and get some readjustment or rearrangement. He should have to discharge the onus of proving what might be fair and equitable and just. The extension or compromise or scheme is set aside; the farmer is back where he started, and in addition to any other remedy the creditor might have, he must start all over again. This is the third round for him. The farmer has brought him in the first time. The creditor has had to bring the farmer in the second time, and now he has to start all over again. It is making it too difficult and it is increasing the hardships already manifest in the operation and administration of this act. It adds to the long delays that are

inherent in the act as drafted. The onus of proof is on the creditor. It seems to me that is an unreasonable provision. I contend that in this extension we are providing another strong argument for the repeal of this act as soon as possible, at least in Ontario. I am sure the operation of this act under these expanded and amended provisions will create a deep sense of injustice. They will cause delays and add expense to the proceedings. This amendment was designed to provide effective machinery for dealing with the dishonest farmer. I repeat what I said yesterday that we in the house cannot undertake to make judicial decisions with respect to particular cases; we can only put in the law such provisions as enable a judge, taking into account all the circumstances, to render a decision fair to both parties in the case.

May I point out to him that if the section were changed as suggested, so that once the debtor was in default he would have to satisfy the court that it was through causes beyond his control, there would not be introduced any innovation into the principles of our law generally. In the long run, despite the quips that are frequently made, in ninety-nine per cent of all cases law is common sense. One very well-established fundamental principle of British law is that though the onus of proving anything is generally upon the applicant or the plaintiff, or upon him who asserts, nevertheless, there is a well-defined exception, namely, where the thing is peculiarly within the knowledge of the respondent or the defendant. Let me give a simple illustration. Let me assume that as the Minister of Finance walks out of this building to-night, a stone falls from the top of the building and strikes him on the head or on the shoulders, and he survives. Under the ordinary principles of law, in order to recover against the owner of the building, he would have to show that that stone fell by reason of the negligence of somebody, in other words, that somebody did that which he ought not to have done, or failed to do that which he ought to have done, and that the person so negligent was an employee or the owner of the building. In the very case that I have cited, however, the law makes an exception. It says: No: it is not reasonably possible for the injured person to know Why the stone fell upon him. If a stone falls off a building which a man owns and keeps, it is within his peculiar knowledge what the conditions are, and so the law in that case puts upon the defendant or the respondent the onus of satisfying the court or the judge or jury, as the case may be, that he was not responsible. I have merely tried to illustrate the principle which I say this section ignores.

Having done that, I say that if the minister and the government still feel that the onus should be on the creditor-because it is their legislation-and despite the fact that the creditor is not in a position to know or easily to find out whether or not the debtor is in default by reason of dishonest motive or in consequence of causes beyond his control, then, of course, I have nothing further to say.

If the suggestion contended for is given effect to, this will be the situation. Farmers in Saskatchewan are in [DOT] default of payments owing to certain companies at the present time under proposals confirmed by the board of review. All such companies would have to do would be to prove that the farmer was in default, and unless he at once hired a lawyer and went to court to prove that the default was due to causes beyond his control, he would be subject to an order throwing him into bankruptcy as a matter of course. Hon. members are contending that the onus should be upon him to prove that the default was beyond his control. Surely that should not be the intention. In regard to the suggestion of the last speaker, a great many bankruptcy offences are mostly within the sole knowledge of the person whom it is sought to throw into bankruptcy: for example, trading after he knew he was insolvent. That is proved out of his own mouth by examining the insolvent for discovery. So when we give to creditors the right to throw into bankruptcy farmers who otherwise could not be thrown into bankruptcy, there should be some protection given to them. When the farmer is in such a condition as to be unable to pay his debts he should not be required to travel long distances and hire a lawyer to prevent his being thrown into bankruptcy.
I uphold the Minister of Finance in his attitude on this point, but I have enough sympathy for creditors in these times to think that they should not be required to make any more applications than are necessary.

Farmers' Creditors Act
far as the present board in cutting down debts, and orders were made which everyone knows now cannot be carried out. Farmers took advantage of that remedial legislation to get as much relief as they could under that law provided for their benefit. But everyone knows that they cannot carry out the orders made. Under the amendment proposed by some hon. members they will be thrown into bankruptcy unless they can go where the court sits and hire a lawyer to prove that the default is beyond their control. I suggest that if the creditor wants to throw the farmer into bankruptcy, which apart from these special provisions he has no right to do, the onus should be on him to prove the essential points, just as, if he wanted to throw a trader into bankruptcy, he must prove the act of bankruptcy. If a bankruptcy order is sought against a trader by reason of his having traded after he became insolvent there would have to be proof of the offence. The trader is not required to prove that he was solvent all the time he was trading. The creditor must prove his case before he can get an order. In the case of the farmer it was carefully provided in the Bankruptcy Act that he could not be put into bankruptcy, no matter how much he owed or how wrongly he acted.

subtopic: BOARDS OF REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILING PROPOSALS, ETC.

What we are asked to do here is to say that if a farmer takes advantage of an act for the adjustment of his debts and then cannot carry out the arrangement he shall be thrown into bankruptcy unless he can prove that it was not his fault. That I say is giving to creditors a right which the act never intended them to have.
As the hon. member for Leeds pointed out, the creditor is forced, in the amendment actually before us, to take it in two stages: first to apply for an order annulling the composition, which order would constitute an act of bankruptcy, and then to apply for the bankruptcy order. In order to avoid the necessity of this second application I would suggest that something be added at the end of subsection 2 providing that the court, having found the creditor to have proved his case and having made such order of annulment, might thereupon declare the farmer bankrupt, so preventing the necessity for a second application.

These defaulters fall into two classes; those unable to fulfil the terms, and those unwilling to do so. The Minister of Finance was very clear both last night and to-day in pointing out that the object of this amendment is to reach the people who were dishonestly refusing to pay when in a position to do so. I think the latter class will be admitted to be by far the minority of the debtors. Now the amendment clearly places upon the creditor the onus for initiating proceedings to annul the composition. Otherwise he would not initiate the proceedings, and if he has such knowledge or information he is the person who should be obliged to prove that. subtopic: CONFIRMATION OF CERTAIN AGREEMENTS BETWEEN DOMINION GOVERNMENT AND PROVINCES OF MANITOBA, SASKATCHEWAN AND ALBERTA
speechtext: The purpose of the bill was explained. This bill is to confirm supplementary agreements which have been signed by the dominion government, represented by the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) and by the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba. Under the statutes transferring the natural resources to the three western provinces the interests of the dominion in all lands, mines and minerals were transferred to the crown in the right of the respective provinces. But apparently some doubt has been raised in the minds of some of the provincial authorities as to whether it is clear that the transfer included the waters and water powers. This bill is merely to remove those doubts. The agreements have been signed by the three provinces and by the Minister of Mines and Resources, and the legislatures of the three provinces have confirmed the agreements. There cannot be any change accorded to them, and we are not losing anything. It is rather to accede to the wishes of the legal officers of the provinces so that no doubt should exist.

subtopic: CONFIRMATION OF CERTAIN AGREEMENTS BETWEEN DOMINION GOVERNMENT AND PROVINCES OF MANITOBA, SASKATCHEWAN AND ALBERTA

speechtext:
No. The agreement covers just the point mentioned by my colleague the Minister of Justice, and another one relating to conservation of gas and oil in the Turner valley. The first point is to make it clear that waters and water powers were transferred to the provinces when the natural resources generally were transferred. I think our law officers held that the water powers and waters are included in the term "lands"; but apparently there is some doubt in the
IM>. Stirling,]
minds of the legal officers advising the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan particularly, and to put the matter beyond any question the supplementary agreement was entered into.
On the other point, as to conservation, the transfer provided that resources which had been alienated or disposed of by the federal government by contract or licence prior to the transfer should not be disturbed except by regulations or changes which would apply generally throughout the province. That, I assume was to guard against any possibility of discrimination. However, it was found by the Alberta government that it was desirable to put into effect certain conservation policies in the Turner valley, which, as hon. members know, is the site of a crude oil field in Alberta. The first drillings developed gas, from which naphtha and some other oils were taken. Later the crude oil field developed. But the value of the crude oil wells depends in a large measure upon the pressure of gas that may be retained several thousand feet down in the earth. The Alberta government wished to put into effect a policy which would conserve or control the escape of this gas; that is, that they could say to individuals or companies, You must take steps to prevent this gas from escaping and thus lowering the pressure. In 1932 the Alberta legislature passed an act, known as the Turner Valley Gas Conservation Act, to effect this purpose. According to the information supplied to me, at least ninety per cent of the operators in the Turner valley favoured that legislation; but there were one or two, one particularly, who took exception to it. The question was carried to the supreme court, and the supreme court declared that under the transfer agreement the province did not have the power to make such regulations unless it made them to apply generally over the whole province. So there was a condition that, for instance, in another oil field at Wainwright the province did not wish to apply these particular policies of conservation because it was thought the result would be detrimental to the operators. Consequently what is sought in this bill is to modify or change the agreement, giving the province of Alberta the power to deal with this particular condition which exists in the Turner valley. According to the information given to me, as I have stated, that commends itself to the judgment of an overwhelming majority of the operators in the Turner valley. Only one or two take exception to it. The technical officials of the Department of Mines and Resources have examined into the matter, and they commend

Natural Resources
it strongly as a necessary step to maintain as long as possible the life of this Turner valley oil field.

subtopic: CONFIRMATION OF CERTAIN AGREEMENTS BETWEEN DOMINION GOVERNMENT AND PROVINCES OF MANITOBA, SASKATCHEWAN AND ALBERTA
speechtext:
By a paragraph of the original transfer agreement,
which has been ratified by the imperial parliament, it was agreed that the provisions of the said agreement might be varied by an agreement confirmed by concurrent statutes of the parliament of Canada and of the legislature of the province. subtopic: CONFIRMATION OF CERTAIN AGREEMENTS BETWEEN DOMINION GOVERNMENT AND PROVINCES OF MANITOBA, SASKATCHEWAN AND ALBERTA

subtopic: CONFIRMATION OF CERTAIN AGREEMENTS BETWEEN DOMINION GOVERNMENT AND PROVINCES OF MANITOBA, SASKATCHEWAN AND ALBERTA
speechtext: I just want to find out what rights were left with this government in connection with the Turner valley.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONFIRMATION OF CERTAIN AGREEMENTS BETWEEN DOMINION GOVERNMENT AND PROVINCES OF MANITOBA, SASKATCHEWAN AND ALBERTA
speechtext: I cannot add anything more to what my hon. friend has said in that connection.

subtopic: CONFIRMATION OF CERTAIN AGREEMENTS BETWEEN DOMINION GOVERNMENT AND PROVINCES OF MANITOBA, SASKATCHEWAN AND ALBERTA
speechtext: I have probably failed to make my point clear. The Alberta government, through the legislature of that province, can bring in conservation regulations, if I may describe them in that way, but under the original transfer agreement those regulations must be made to apply generally over the whole province. What they wish is to obtain power to pass regulations not applicable to the whole province; in other words, they wisli regulations to apply to a particular area because in a peculiar way that area requires them. Under the judgment of the supreme court in 1933 they have not that power. As a matter of fact, the Alberta legislature thought it had the power, and the previous government of that province passed the act to which I referred a moment ago, dealing with the conservation of the Turner valley gas. The court here, however, held that the legislature did not have power to pass such an act unless it applied generally over the whole province, which was not what they desired. This amended agreement seeks to give the government of Alberta, through its legislature, power to make regulations which may apply only to the Turner valley situation.

subtopic: CONFIRMATION OF CERTAIN AGREEMENTS BETWEEN DOMINION GOVERNMENT AND PROVINCES OF MANITOBA, SASKATCHEWAN AND ALBERTA
speechtext: It is a difficult point.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONFIRMATION OF CERTAIN AGREEMENTS BETWEEN DOMINION GOVERNMENT AND PROVINCES OF MANITOBA, SASKATCHEWAN AND ALBERTA
speechtext:
May I add this, which I read in the agreement with Alberta, with regal'd to the matter of the Turner valley:
-by paragraph 2 of the said natifral resources transfer agreement the province agreed that it would carry out, in accordance with the terms thereof, every contract to purchase or lease any crown lands, mines or minerals and

every other arrangement whereby any person had become entitled to any interest therein as against the crown, and further agreed not to affect or alter any term of any such contract to purchase, lease or other arrangement by legislation or otherwise, except either with the consent of all the parties thereto, other than Canada, or in so far as any legislation may apply generally to all similar agreements relating to lands, mines or minerals in the province or to interests therein, irrespective of who might be the parties thereto;-
In other words, the Dominion of Canada bound the province at the time so that the province would not alter any term of any contract with any party unless all the parties were agreed or unless such alteration by legislation would apply generally to all agreements relating to lands, mines or minerals, irrespective of the place or the person affected. Apparently this worked some injury in that particular district, and paragraph 2 is to be amended by adding these words:
-or is legislation relating to the conservation of oil resources or gas resources or both by the control or regulation of the production of oil or gas or both, whether by restriction or prohibition and whether generally or with respect to any specified area or any specified well or wells or by repressuring of any oil field, gas field or oil-gas field, and, incidentally thereto, providing for the compulsory purchase of any well or wells.
That will enable the province to make new arrangements with regard to certain wells in a specified area, which it could not do under the original agreement.

speechtext: I am entirely in accord with this bill except in one respect. This bill amends a very important act, and for that reason it has been scrutinized closely by the law officers of the crown. The fear is that amendments of this type will alter the basic character of the Railway Act. While this bill was in committee, the word "land" in line 12 was struck out. The law officers feel that if this amendment is allowed to stand it will set a precedent and have the tendency to turn the railway board into a court for small claims. The board does deal with land damages, and if the word "land" is allowed to remain in the bill, the provisions of the bill would be consistent with the purposes for which the board was created. subtopic: AMENDMENT OF PROVISION RESPECTING PROHIBITED CLASSES
speechtext:
I move:
That the order for resuming adjourned debate on second reading of Bill No. 38 be discharged and an order for the second reading of the said bill be substituted therefor.

Motion agreed to.
Mr. A. \V. NEILL (Comox-Alberni) moved the second reading of Bill No. 38, to amend the Immigration Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the number of this bill is 38, and its title, "an act to amend the Immigration Act." It has no connection whatever, express or implied, with Bill No. 11, although some member made some comparison between the two, but there is no connection at all. Bill No. 11, if you compare it with this bill, might be allied in the sense that two people travelling in the same train to a common destination could be said to be allied, although they would hardly be called allies because they might be utterly antagonistic in aim and outlook.
Bill No 11 is an act respecting Japanese immigration, and it definitely and specifically,
Immigration Act

by name, excludes Japanese nationals from entering Canada. The word "excludes" is not used, but that is the effect, and it is admitted to be so.
Bill No. 38, which is now before the house for second reading, and is an act to amend the Immigration Act, has nothing to do with that at all. It makes no reference to excluding anybody by name or by race. It does not even restrict orientals alone but applies to seventy-four per cent of the world's population, comprising many races, and, of course, an enormous population. It does not even stop them from entering Canada if they comply with certain conditions laid down in the bill.
I shall now explain the bill. It amends the principle that has been in our Immigration Act now for twenty-five years. I refer to section 3 of the Immigration Act, chapter 93 of the revised statutes of Canada, paragraph (t) of which provides that among those who are prohibited immigrants are those over fifteen years of age physically capable of reading who cannot read the English or French language or some other language or dialect. That is our law to-day and has been for many years. This bill simply goes a very little further, makes a very fair amplification of the same principle, and says in addition that the language which they use must be commonly spoken by and native to the people of some country or some political division in Europe. That is the only change it makes. It only brings us in Canada into line with Australia and New Zealand, of which I shall speak later.
Moreover, this is what I might call a legislative olive branch. When the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), speaking on the second reading of Bill No. 11, indicated the opposition of his government to that bill, I considered the situation. In politics I think it is a good axiom, when you cannot get the right remedy for the grievance of which you complain, while not relaxing your determination to get it, to accept such minor measure as you can get as a palliative for the time being, and use that as a stepping-stone to obtain a greater measure of justice which no doubt time will bring. So in this bill I gathered up all the objections, all the prejudices, all the propaganda, all the opposition to Bill No. 11, and I said: I think the government is wrong; but the government is in the majority, and the government majority must rule. Therefore let us abandon this bill for the moment until the government is perhaps better informed by the result of a general election-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF PROVISION RESPECTING PROHIBITED CLASSES
speechtext: Is Bill No. 11 abandoned?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF PROVISION RESPECTING PROHIBITED CLASSES
speechtext:
For the moment. We are dealing now with Bill No. 38. So I said: Let us wait until the government is better informed as a result of a general election, which in British Columbia at any rate will show very definitely what the wishes of the people are. My definition of democracy-it may be a wrong one-at least contains this provision, that the government, those who govern, should govern according to the wishes of the governed, provided that their wishes are sufficiently and definitely and legally expressed. And so we say: Abandon for the moment the proper principle contained in Bill No. 11 and adopt this lesser measure of a totally different kind, which will in some measure placate the people of British Columbia, whose views have been expressed very plainly.
I hold in my hand a summary of the presentations made by the Pattullo government of British Columbia to the Rowell commission. It summarizes fifteen important items, and the one which they apparently deemed of sufficient importance to put first is this:
Oriental immigration into Canada should be prohibited, and as many orientals as possible returned to their home countries.
Then here I have a resolution passed within the last few weeks by the council of the city of Vancouver, a Conservative minded body. This is not the chronic obsession of some solitary member, but expresses the feeling of the people of British Columbia as reflected in a resolution passed by the city council of the largest city in the province and the third largest city in Canada. They ask that the dominion parliament enact legislation to prevent a further influx of these people into . our country.
This bill asks nothing like that at all. It does not ask that these people should be sent home or that they should be excluded, it asks simply that the immigrants shall be restricted to those who can read the language indicated. While I am anxious to secure the best that can be obtained for the people of British Columbia, in friendliness to the government, too, I should be glad to see them accept this bill because it is a way out of the unpopularity that will accrue to them if they reject Bill No. 11 without accepting some reasonable substitute.
It is customaiy, in introducing a bill, to anticipate the objections that will be made against it and to defend the bill against such attacks, but in this case I am at a loss because I do not see how anybody can object to this bill. I cannot see in it anything to which anyone could take exception.

Immigration Act
One of the charge? made against Bill No. 11 was that it was aimed at Japan, and certainly it was. But this bill is nothing of that kind at all. Japan is not mentioned first or last, neither directly nor indirectly, nor by inference. The restriction is entirely general, and general to such an extent that, as I say, it applies to seventy-four per cent of the world's population. The most sensitive pro-Jap advocate could not find any loophole for complaint in this bill.
Another objection made was that it touched the pride of the Japanese nation; that the word "exclusion" was antagonistic to their pride. That expression which I have heard for the last seventeen years is a mere subterfuge, a mere diplomatic phrase, that is trotted out when it suits them. It is wholly incompatible with what we have observed of their ideals in diplomatic and other fields, of their sense of their obligations, and so forth. It is a mere phrase used where convenient. However, I am willing for the moment to accept it at the face value. It utterly falls down as applied to Bill No. 38, because this bill contains no reference to exclusion. Under the bill, in fact, it is impossible totally to exclude anybody, because it leaves the door open to those who can read the English or French language; we go further in our gracious hospitality, and we will take in anyone, even from the continent of Europe, who can read any language that is current there. Surely that is neither a hard nor an unreasonable condition considering the condition of the world to-day; and it is of almost universal application.
Another argument was-I have heard it again and again, and I have heard it cited by the Prime Minister-that Japan particularly objected to that phase of any exclusion because it was aimed at them specifically. They said they would not mind at all if it was general and took in all nations; but their pride, or what they call their pride, was touched because they were specifically named. If that is the case, this bill is right into their hand; it should suit them. We do not exclude anybody, but we restrict immigration- from where? From India-our own vast domain of India-from China, Japan, South America, the Malay peninsula and those countries in the neighbourhood, Siam and Borneo, constituting a large number both in races and in population. In 1922, when the restriction resolution was before the house, the Hon. Charles Stewart was minister of immigration. The resolution called for the exclusion of orientals. Mr. Stewart introduced an amendment which struck out the word "exclusion" and substituted the words "effective restriction."
I asked the Prime Minister of the day, who was the same gentlemen who now occupies that position, if we could understand by that such a measure of restriction as, for instance, was used in Australia, and he assured me that that would be the case. I have the quotation if it is needed. Well, we have not got so far yet. Sixteen years have passed; we have been looking for a phrase to meet the situation, and I suggest we have it now. This bill does that. It gives us an effective restriction equivalent to that in Australia without using the words "total exclusion."
We have precedents. The lawyers are great on precedents; they want to go slow until they see that a thing has been done before. We have a precedent of our own. For twenty-five years an educational test has been administered to people coming in. We have the precedent of Australia. This is what the Australian act says with regard to prohibited classes:
Any person who fails to pass the dictation test:
That is to say, who, when an officer or person duly authorized in writing by an officer dictates to him not less than fifty words in any prescribed language, fails to write them out in that language in the presence of the officer or authorized person.
It will be noticed that this goes much further than my bill, because it meahs any language at all, whereas I would be satisfied with any language of Europe. Their law requires any language prescribed by the government, and the government always takes great care to prescribe a language in which the immigrant cannot qualify. For instance, if he can speak six languages they would try him with the seventh, in which he would be bound to fail. I may say that in New Zealand the law is the same, but with this difference, that there they allow anyone to qualify if he can write fifty words in any language of Europe, whereas in Australia it is just "any language."
There is an incident connected with that which may be of interest to our Scotch friends in the house. Originally in Australia the words were also "any language of Europe"; but apparently some Scotsman got himself appointed inspector, and from some weird sense of humour he set a Chinaman to write out fifty words in Gaelic as being a prescribed language of Europe. The case will be found in the law books of 1905, Rex v. Wilson. But the Supreme Court of Australia decided that Gaelic was not a "language of Europe," very much t'o the disgust of the Scotch contingent, and there was very nearly a revolution. Kilts were donned and sporrans

Immigration Act

were waved-or whatever you do with sporrans-claymores were drawn and the fiery cross was sent abroad in the land. The government realized the danger of the situation, and capitulated, and at the next session of the house they changed the act to read "any language," which allowed the Gaelic brand of language to be used also. But in New Zealand it is "any language of Europe," and that is all I ask in connection with this bill.
Take another precedent, affecting the East Indians, those who live in India. They are our own fellow citizens, and some of them qualify ethnologically as being Aryans and therefore white men; but we prohibit them from coming into Canada, and the way in which we do it is by the barest subterfuge. We say they cannot come in unless they come in a ship proceeding directly from the port of embarkation to the port of debarkation in Canada, and moreover they must come on a through passage ticket. Then we take steps to see they cannot get a through passage ticket. It is done as simply and obviously as that. They might complain about it; but still that is the way we do it; that is the precedent.
I cannot think of any other objection. It is sanctioned by our own immigration law; it is sanctioned by our custom as regards the East Ihdians; it has been the law of New Zealand and Australia for at least thirty years. As I said, it is an olive branch, and it is also a test of the sincerity of the Japanese who are opposing this bill. We have met every objection to Bill No. 11, and have obviated it-. I ask the house to note also that there is in the bill a provision that it will not come into effect until July, 1939, which gives ample time for the amenities of diplomacy to come into operation and also to make such arrangements that immigrants on the water would not be incommoded, but would have ample time.
To sum up; the law is of general application. It has been in force thirty years in the sister dominions of New Zealand and Australia. It is merely idle talk to say that we must not do this lest we offend one small nation comprising seven per cent of seventy-four per cent of the world population, and now subject to a similar restriction in these other dominions. If the house, and of course the government, will accept this bill I would be willing, with the consent of those hon. members who have promised me their support of Bill No. 11, to withdraw it. But I would say this to the government: British Columbia wants Bill No. 11 and will not be satisfied until

she gets it, and she will get it after she has expressed herself sufficiently strongly at the election. But for the moment this bill would meet the situation and would meet a very serious situation in British Columbia. I cannot too strongly impress upon the house and the government how serious that situation is. It is all very well as long as things are going along smoothly, but there is a very strong and bitter undercurrent about this matter. You may gauge its importance when you find the city council of Vancouver taking it up, and every paper carries resolutions passed by this or that body along the same line. British Columbia will not be satisfied with anything but Bill No. 11. But for the moment, for the sake of peace, for the sake of the representations made by the Prime Minister and the views he expressed, founded upon what he says is his greater and inner knowledge of international matters, it would be a reasonable and fair compromise to accept this bill and satisfy British Columbia for the moment, and it would be a measure of justice. I earnestly commend it to the consideration of the government and of the house.

Mr. Speaker, on a point of order, before we proceed any further, the rules of the house as adopted on June 14, 1923, among other provisions contain the following:
In the text of the bill, on the left hand page, new matter shall be indicated by such typographical means as may best suit the varying circumstances of each case, such as brackets, italics, underlining, asterisks, etc. Opposite each clause, on the right hand page, the enactment amended thereby, or so much thereof as is essential, shall be printed with the proposed changes to be made therein similarly indicated.
The bill that the house has before it has nothing at all opposite the clause on the right hand page. It is true that on the left hand side new matter is underlined; but the opposite page does not contain what the rules state should be complied with, namely so much of the enactment as is essential to be printed with the proposed changes to be made therein similarly indicated. Before we proceed further, I would ask your honour to give a ruling on the point whether the bill does comply with the rules of the house.

On the point of order, I submit that the bill does comply with the essential feature of the rule, which is that changes shall be indicated by such typographical means as may best suit the varying circumstances of

Immigration Act
each case, such as brackets, italics, underlining and so on. That is done in the bill before us. The part which the Prime Minister says is left out is the "explanatory notes" on the right hand page, but that omission in so sense interferes with the essential part of the bill. The bill is so simple that I suppose the law clerk who drew it-I did not draw it-thought it unnecessary to put, in explanatory notes, what is so obvious. A number of bills have gone through the house since that rule was made and they have had no explanatory notes on the right hand page, the reason being I have no doubt, that the bills were so obvious as to render such explanations unnecessary. I would call attention to page 348 of the rules, subsection (3) of paragraph 7:
When a clause repeals an existing section, subsection or other minor division of a section, that section, subsection or division, or so much thereof as is essential, shall be printed opposite the clause.
The purpose of the explanatory notes on the right hand side of the bill is to enable us to see what we are amending. In this instance we are not striking out anything in order to substitute something else, and therefore it was impossible to print on the right hand page the provision to be struck out-impossible for the simple reason that nothing was being struck out. I have not looked up other bills on the file; but hon. members will find, on looking through their files, case after case where nothing is printed on the right hand page of the bill.
