speechtext:
This is Bill No. 11. Having been defeated on one front, I have to fall back upon a line of defence which I hope will be more acceptable to the government. When the bill came up last on March 22, I had spoken for a minute and a half before the hour had elapsed. A member on the government side, writing home to British Columbia, had this to say in his news notes:
It was expected that a vote would take place }n this but Mr. Neill, who rose to speak at 3ve minutes to nine refused to end his remarks and let the vote take place.
That statement is neither correct nor fair. It was not five minutes to nine but one and a half minutes, as shown by the records of the house and of Hansard. It is not fair, because it says I refused to let the vote be taken. I refused to let the bill be defeated at that time for the reason I shall give. This bill was brought up for second reading on February 17; it was spoken to by a number of hon. members in its favour, and then the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) spoke against it and moved the adjournment of the debate. Subsequently it came up on three or four different occasions, when four and two and three hon. members respectively, on the government side spoke until the time elapsed. They were all against the bill, with the exception of the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church), who spoke for a few minutes. It was well known that the government intended to defeat
CMr. Speaker.]
the bill, because the Prime Minister told us at the beginning that he could not accept it. That would be the end of the bill for this session. As it was going to be defeated it did not make much difference whether it were defeated three weeks ago or to-day, but it was not fair that it should go out to the world after nine men spoke against it-I do not say they used sound arguments, but they did argue against it-and with no attempt being made to rebut their arguments. I did not want the bill to go to defeat without the house and country being informed as to the rebuttal arguments which could be put forward. That is important because this will not be the end of this bill; the fight will be carried to the next election. When the next election comes, I shall have ample time to visit the electorate of Vancouver island and the lower mainland and explain the situation to them fully. I am afraid some hon. members of the government party will have some difficulty in squaring themselves with their constituencies. They may say, "Yes, I voted for it, but the government would not permit it to carry." But they should have used their influence with their party to allow it to pass.
Let us deal now with some of the reasons alleged against the bill. First we were told: Do not worry about this bill; we will give you a committee of investigation to find out whether orientals are coming in illegally. But who composed the committee? A gentleman from Ottawa, and the head of the police department of Vancouver and of the immigration department, the two men on whom blame would rest if it were discovered that there had been any illegal entry. Human nature is the same in British Columbia as anywhere else. Does anyone think these men were going to condemn themselves? The real way to go about it, if there were to be an investigation along these lines, would be to appoint a retired supreme court judge; there are several available in British Columbia. But the really effective way to get practical results would be to do as was done in the war- have all orientals registered. That is no disgrace; I had to register, along with other people, and produce my registration card on demand. If that were done it would be a simple and ready test; for if any oriental could not show that he was in the country legally he would have no card.
On March 22 the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) said he would endorse the bill if a proviso were put in that it should not come into effect until July, 1939. I hereby accept that condition, and hope for his support.

Japanese Immigration
The bill could easily have passed but for the announcement by the Prime Minister that the government was against it. I make full allowance for the inner knowledge that the Prime Minister has of international affairs, but I think he might have given us some information, lifted the curtain to some extent. When we compare the situation in Great Britain, where members of parliament, even cabinet ministers, rise in their places and speak with almost brutal frankness regarding the conduct of nations in Europe, even in the present strained situation, I think we might have had some explanation of the reason why it was so urgent that this bill be, not passed. I submit that the reasons given W'ere inadequate. We were told that it was calculated to provoke war. That is a very strong statement, one which, I think, is hardly justified. If we were proposing something unfair to the Japanese nation, to take some territory away from them, or some of their rights, or some of their land in British Columbia, or to deport them, there might have been some justification. But what are we doing? We are seeking only to regain control of our own immigration, with which we should never have parted. To dd so was a foolish thing, done by no other nation in the world. How can any nation, Japan or any other, object to our taking back control of our own affairs? One might as well complain because his neighbour comes and asks for the return of the lawn-mower that one borrowed from him.
Then it was suggested by the Prime Minister that as the immigration was so small- I think he put it at about 130-it was not worth going to war over, or provoking war over. Well, I can turn that argument roundabout. If the number of immigrants were only 130-it is not so, but let us assume that it was-is it worth Japan's while under present conditions to go to war over it, especially when they know that we are entirely within our rights?
The Prime Minister admitted, as reported at page 569 of Hansard, that Japan and China should be treated on an equality. But the principal argument alleged was that Japan might not like the action proposed. That is a poor reason. If we are going to be governed along those lines, we shall have to ask Japan if we have her permission to fortify British Columbia. I am sure she would not like that either.
Nations often do things that other nations do not like. The United States periodically raise their tariff against us; we do not like it. but I have heard it said often in this house that it is the right of the United
States to do that. The United States at one time imposed a quota against immigration from Canada; we did not like it but we knew it was their right. How ready we are to take offence against British public men expressing opinions concerning our affairs! Let one of even humble capacity travelling through Canada as a tourist make some casual observation touching upon the way we govern ourselves, and we rise up in arms and almost wave the bloody sword and say we will not be dominated by Downing street; let the British people mind their own business. I have often blushed at the way in which we have treated British visitors. But no offence is taken; Britain smiles and says:	They
are a young nation; they will learn better as they get older. Apparently it is right and proper that we should insult our friends but accept insults from other nations. Let me quote a dispatch * from Tokyo. This comes through the Associated Press; it is no propaganda of mine got in some hole-and-corner way:
Tokyo, March 7-Foreign Minister Koki Hirota declared in the Diet to-day that American-born Japanese, even though living in America, "should be educated as Japanese."
The statement was in reply to questions from Bunji Suzuki, labour leader, who asked if the government had any educational policy for those of the " second generation."
Hirota replied: "A majority of Japanese born in the United States in recent years cancelled Japanese citizenship. They must receive an American education. But they remain Japanese, and they should be educated as Japanese in order to retain Japanese virtues. For this purpose the semi-official migration association keeps close connection with them."
We know what that means. It means that Japanese bom in this country are maintaining a dual nationality. They leave our schools and get educated in their own schools. I wonder whether we would tolerate that if it were proposed in the British parliament, for instance.
Both the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) referred to what happened in the United States. What did happen? In 1924 the United States put a complete ban upon oriental immigration, and both hon. gentlemen quoted what Japan said at that time, with the vague suggestion that we had better be careful. That was all that was said, and what happened; I asked the Minister of Mines and Resources? Just exactly nothing happened. Even trade continued to flow along the usual lines between Japan and the United States. Nothing happened because they knew the United States were well within their rights. Did they go to

Japanese Immigration

war with the United States over that? They did not. The other day Brazil did the same thing. Japan made one of these infamous gentleman's agreements with Brazil, and I see that Brazil has become fed up with it and has passed a law cancelling the gentleman's agreement, imposing a very effective restriction against the Japanese. Did they go to war with Brazil over that? They did not. We read in the papers the other day that the government of Panama issued a most unfriendly, almost hostile, order that no Japanese fishermen were to come within so many miles of the coast of that country or they would blow them up. That is going pretty far; I would call that an unfriendly act. Did they go to war over that? They did not. Did they go to war with South Africa when that country negotiated a total exclusion agreement? Did they go to war with Australia or New Zealand when they did the same thing? They did not. If the Japanese swallow exclusion by these other countries but become insulted when Canada does the same thing, I say that is evidence of their insincerity, unsupported by any claim in international relationship or anything that governs as between friendly nations. When they say their pride will not permit them to be excluded, they are just as insincere as they are with all their talk about the loyalty of second generation Japanese. It comes out in their own parliament that they are arranging to have these second generation Japanese remain Japanese in thought and education.
Apparently the government is too apt to look at the Japanese angle and none other. Let us forget the Japanese viewpoint for a moment. Let us consider Canada; let us consider British Columbia, which will be a bloody shambles if there is a war in the Pacific. Let us think of that. Let us think of the Chinese viewpoint. The other day on the second reading of this bill the Prime Minister said that nations were slow to forget any injuries they thought they had sustained. Quite so; and he applied that to Japan. It also applies to China, does it not? Let us consider the Chinese viewpoint. In days to come we might be glad if we do something to make the Chinese forget that for sixteen years they have been excluded from Canada entirely, while we have let in Japanese. We have entirely excluded East Indians but have allowed Japanese to come in. It might be a good thing if we did something to make China forget that. It would be a fine gesture, would it not, not to give them any favour but to put the Japanese on equality with the Chinese, to put the two countries on the same basis. And it might be a good idea if we

could help China to forget the way in which our minister treated them. We sent to Japan an infirm, old man, unversed in diplomacy, not acquainted with the country, and he allowed himself to be loaded up to the hilt with Japanese propaganda. Then he came back and disseminated it throughout Canada. It was not a globe-trotting tourist who could be passed by with a smile; he was our accredited minister. Do you think China has forgotten that? If we passed this bill it would be a gesture which would help them to forget it.
Perhaps it is a question of expediency; perhaps it is the goddess of expediency that governs. Let us take her off her pedestal and treat everybody on the same basis; let us check off our minister and treat them all alike. If expediency is to govern, by all means let us play with China, because Japan will not be a powerful nation for very much longer, and she does not know the meaning of the word gratitude. China will come back a strong, virile, united nation, with a sense of gratitude to those who have been her friends, and offering an enormous potential market of four hundred million people to take our goods. With no country in the world is it so dangerous to adopt an attitude of not standing up for your rights as it is with Japan. The school bully always gets more and more aggressive, pushing around people who do not want to quarrel with him, until some small boy half his size punches him on the nose and then everyone wonders why someone did not do it before. We cannot afford to adopt an attitude like that. Let us, as the French say, "Ayez du courage"; let us stand upon our own feet. "Dare to be a Daniel; dare to stand alone; dare to have a purpose firm." We need not be truculent; but let us stand up for our rights. That is the best way by which to bring about peace abroad and prosperity at home.
I have been accused of trying to stir up racial prejudice. Not at all; I have only pointed out the impossibility of assimilating such an alien race. One of the greatest obstacles to assimilation is the lack of marriage between the two races. The other day I saw a record of the births of one hundred thousand Canadian children; of that number I think only seven were Eurasian, and nearly all of those were the issue of white individuals and Chinese, not Japs. I think there was only one or possibly two out of the one hundred thousand born to white and Japanese parents. They do not want to marry us and we do not want to marry them. Look at Europe, where for centuries the Greek and the Turk have

Northwest Territories-Furs
lived together in enmity. The best that civilization has been able to do is to move them by the hundreds of thousands back to where they came from. Look at the Arabs and Jews in Palestine, where the best solution that can be devised by the British government is to put a fence down the middle of the country and keep each race on its own side. Yet we talk about assimilating these people.
There is another point, perhaps the most important of all. A new policy has been developed in the countries of the world. It is now considered right and proper for a nation to interfere in the affairs of another nation, provided the second nation contains enough nationals of the first nation. That is what happened in Austria; that is what will happen in Czechoslovakia. Never in the world has there been such a coup d'etat as occurred in Austria the other day, because they had so many German sympathizers in that country ready to take action. Suppose we should be told some day that because Japan had thirty thousand nationals in British Columbia she insisted that they must be given the vote and all the privileges our own citizens possess, the opportunity to become lawyers, doctors and all the rest of it. What would we do about that?
Will the government meet the wishes of British Columbia or defy them? Will the government say that it is going to govern without regard to the wishes of those governed? That is not democracy; that is autocracy.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING SHIPMENT OR TAKING OUT OF FURS WITHOUT PROPER AUTHORITY

speechtext: Hon. T. A. CRERAR (Minister of Mines and Resources) moved the second reading of Bill No. 110, to amend the Northwest Territories Act.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING SHIPMENT OR TAKING OUT OF FURS WITHOUT PROPER AUTHORITY
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING SHIPMENT OR TAKING OUT OF FURS WITHOUT PROPER AUTHORITY
speechtext:
The purpose of the bill, Mr. Speaker, is to enable the government, through the council which administers the Northwest Territories, to exercise a closer control over the export or movement of furs from the Northwest Territories to any of the provinces. Abuses in this respect have developed during the last few years on account of the increasing number of people going into the territories and the augmented use of airplanes for transportation both into and out of the territories. Trappers frequently are taken to their trapping grounds by airplane and are brought out at the end of the season by the same method.
In 1927 the Northwest Territories Act was amended to provide that any one taking furs out of the territories must obtain a permit. A year or two later regulations establishing the charge that would be levied, was passed. This corresponds to the royalties imposed by every province in Canada on the taking of furs. This method worked very well, but, as I said a moment ago. the development in airplane transportation has led to evasions of the tax. It is suspected that much of the fur is being taken out without the necessary fee being paid.
This bill seeks to overcome this trouble by applying the principle applied by the Department of National Revenue in connection with excise collections. There is being added to the act a new section, the first clause of which reads:
A judge of the exchequer court of Canada shall grant a writ of assistance upon application made to him for that purpose by His Majesty's attorney general of Canada.
That is similar to the powers granted in connection with the administration of the Excise Act, only in that instance the writ of assistance may be secured from a judge
Northwest Territories-Furs

other than a judge of the exchequer court. Under authority of this writ of assistance the baggage of a passenger who is suspected of bringing out furs illegally may be searched. Other provisions in the amendment deal with the disposal of the furs and the vehicle by which they are being transported. Subsection 4 provides that sections 171 to 184 inclusive of the Customs Act shall apply. These sections would provide for the disposal of a vehicle that may be impounded.
The necessity of this provision is emphasized by the fact that there are practically only two airplane bases at which airplanes from the Northwest Territories would land. One is at Prince Albert in Saskatchewan and the other is at Cooking Lake, about fifteen or eighteen miles from Edmonton. When a trapper is suspected of bringing out furs illegally, it is impossible to get a regular search warrant to authorize the search of his luggage before he gets away. Once he gets away, it is almost impossible to locate him again. Provisions of this bill would enable prompt action to be taken.
For the information of the house I might say that the total value of the fur catch in the Northwest Territories for 1935-36, the latest figures obtainable, was $1,188,000 in round figures. In 1934-35 the value of the catch was $1,678,000. At the present time the cycle of the fur catch is low, but several years ago the value of the catch ran over $2,000,000. In 1926-27 the value was almost $3,000,000. The revenue from this fur catch amounted to $57,000 in 1938. The revenue in 1936 was $105,000, and in 1935 it reached the highest point in any single year, $146,000. This matter has been receiving the attention of the Department of Justice, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and the Northwest Territories council, and they have come to the conclusion that the best method of dealing with these abuses is by means of the amendment to the act which I am now asking the house to adopt.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING SHIPMENT OR TAKING OUT OF FURS WITHOUT PROPER AUTHORITY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the principle of this bill seems to be to strengthen the powers behind this law and to provide additional facilities for preventing the abuses which apparently have grown up. Assuming, as we must, that the law is sound, I can see no objection to the principle of this bill. There is no question that our laws should be enforced and that we should provide adequate machinery and facilities for that purpose.

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Sanderson in the chair.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING SHIPMENT OR TAKING OUT OF FURS WITHOUT PROPER AUTHORITY
speechtext:

between this bill and the spectacular fur robbery that occurred two years ago somewhere south of Aklavik?

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING SHIPMENT OR TAKING OUT OF FURS WITHOUT PROPER AUTHORITY
speechtext: I do not recall the particulars of the incident to which my hon. friend refers. There may be some connection, but I cannot state definitely at the moment. Furs have been taken out illegally from the territories, and this practice is tending to grow and, I think, will grow still further with the increased use of the airplane. A trapper may go to his trapping ground by airplane, and an airplane brings him out when his trapping season is over. He does not report his furs to the authorities. He comes out, lands his furs at Edmonton, we will say, or Prince Albert, and sells them and there is no way of apprehending him. I am not a legal man and am not familiar with legal phraseology; but I understand that a writ of assistance is a sort of continuing search warrant issued to a particular individual; as I stated a moment ago, the bill has received the careful study not only of the officers of the department but of the mounted police and officers of the justice department as well, and the result of their combined wisdom as to how best to check this evil is the bill now before us.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING SHIPMENT OR TAKING OUT OF FURS WITHOUT PROPER AUTHORITY
speechtext: How, practically, will the trapper go to work? Will he go to an official of the department and ask for permission to export so many furs?

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING SHIPMENT OR TAKING OUT OF FURS WITHOUT PROPER AUTHORITY
speechtext: Yes; he is given a licence unless he is a native of the Northwest Territories. Indians and half-breeds are not required to take out a licence. The trapper is supposed to report his furs out at the expiration of his period of trapping; but in some cases he fails to do so, or he may report only part of his furs and sell the balance, and there is to-day no way of ascertaining whether he is reporting correctly. This provision is to enable a search to be made where it is suspected that a person is selling furs and evading the tax he should pay.

This relates to the Northwest Territories.

New Westminster Harbour

speechtext: But the minister said that the furs coming out of the Northwest Territories would be landed at Edmonton or Prince Albert, and I was wondering if the provincial governments had any jurisdiction, and. if so. if they had made any recommendations to the federal department.

speechtext: No; they have made no recommendations. As a matter of fact, they are not interested in the furs that come out of the Northwest Territories because they do not collect any royalties on such furs. It is purely a matter of interest to the federal administration.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING SHIPMENT OR TAKING OUT OF FURS WITHOUT PROPER AUTHORITY

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING SHIPMENT OR TAKING OUT OF FURS WITHOUT PROPER AUTHORITY
speechtext: He takes out a permit, but before he gets the permit the authorities have to 'be satisfied that the proper tax has been paid.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING SHIPMENT OR TAKING OUT OF FURS WITHOUT PROPER AUTHORITY
speechtext:
Exactly, before he gets the permit ito take it out. Then I notice that the exchequer court is the court that may
issue the writ. Is there any other court having jurisdiction there and authority to issue the writ?

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING SHIPMENT OR TAKING OUT OF FURS WITHOUT PROPER AUTHORITY
speechtext: No.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING SHIPMENT OR TAKING OUT OF FURS WITHOUT PROPER AUTHORITY
speechtext:
No other court or
authority that could exercise the powers outlined in the bill?

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING SHIPMENT OR TAKING OUT OF FURS WITHOUT PROPER AUTHORITY
speechtext: No. In that respect, as I said a few moments ago, this section is a little bit narrower than the similar section in the Customs Act dealing with the excise duty.

Section agreed to.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF BOUNDARIES AND REMUNERATION OF COMMISSIONERS OUT OF HARBOUR REVENUES

speechtext:
Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Transport) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
hat it is expedient to introduce amendments to the New Westminster Harbour Commissioners Act to extend the boundaries of the harbour and to provide remuneration for the services of the commissioners out of harbour revenues.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Sanderson in the chair.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF BOUNDARIES AND REMUNERATION OF COMMISSIONERS OUT OF HARBOUR REVENUES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the bill
founded on the resolution divides itself into two parts, as the resolution indicates. The first part is to include in the boundaries of New Westminster harbour a small area lying between the present jurisdiction of the New Westminster harbour commission and the jurisdiction of the North Fraser harbour commission. This area arises out of a change in the boundaries of the North Fraser harbour commission, and it is desirable to have either one commission or the other have jurisdiction over it.
The second part provides that the governor in council may set up such remuneration for the New Westminster harbour commission as the government may determine. The present situation is somewhat unsatisfactory. No provision is made for paying the commissioners, so the remuneration is obtained through appointing the chairman the commission manager of the port, for which he draws a substantial salary, and I believe that part of his salary is paid by him to his two fellow commissioners. It is believed that it is not desirable to do indirectly a thing which is not provided for in the act. Similar harbour commissioners throughout Canada are paid
New Westminster Harbour

small salaries for their services, and the government believes that the request of the city of New Westminster should be granted and that provision should be made for the remuneration of the harbour commissioners.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF BOUNDARIES AND REMUNERATION OF COMMISSIONERS OUT OF HARBOUR REVENUES
speechtext: Is this an area which at present is in the North Fraser area, and is it going to be put into New Westminster?

subtopic: EXTENSION OF BOUNDARIES AND REMUNERATION OF COMMISSIONERS OUT OF HARBOUR REVENUES
speechtext: No; this is a sort of no-man's land between the two. At one time it was included in the North Fraser harbour commission jurisdiction, but the boundaries of the North Fraser harbour commission jurisdiction were changed some three or four yeras ago, and for some reason that I cannot explain this territory was dropped from the jurisdiction of the North Fraser commission. At the moment it is administered by the Department of Transport, but I believe it should be administered by one or other of the harbour boards, and it seems properly to come within the jurisdiction of the New Westminster harbour commission.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF BOUNDARIES AND REMUNERATION OF COMMISSIONERS OUT OF HARBOUR REVENUES
speechtext: Who now owns it?

subtopic: EXTENSION OF BOUNDARIES AND REMUNERATION OF COMMISSIONERS OUT OF HARBOUR REVENUES
speechtext: It is owned by the crown and administered by the Department of Transport.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF BOUNDARIES AND REMUNERATION OF COMMISSIONERS OUT OF HARBOUR REVENUES
speechtext: Would the minister tell us how many commissioners there are, what their proposed remuneration is, and from what source it will be obtained? Will it be from harbour dues?

subtopic: EXTENSION OF BOUNDARIES AND REMUNERATION OF COMMISSIONERS OUT OF HARBOUR REVENUES
speechtext: There are three commissioners. It is proposed to pay each of the three a small salary from the revenues of the port. The port of New Westminster is, of course, a very busy one-

subtopic: EXTENSION OF BOUNDARIES AND REMUNERATION OF COMMISSIONERS OUT OF HARBOUR REVENUES
speechtext: A free port.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF BOUNDARIES AND REMUNERATION OF COMMISSIONERS OUT OF HARBOUR REVENUES
speechtext:
-and it has substantial
revenues. The business is considerable, and it takes a good deal of the time of the commissioners. It is proposed to pay each of the commissioners a small salary for part-time work.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF BOUNDARIES AND REMUNERATION OF COMMISSIONERS OUT OF HARBOUR REVENUES
speechtext: I assume the remuneration will be paid from charges obtained on freights coming into the harbour, harbour dues.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF BOUNDARIES AND REMUNERATION OF COMMISSIONERS OUT OF HARBOUR REVENUES
speechtext: There are no harbour dues, but there are certain revenues from leaseholds, ships' dues and one thing and another, including wharfage. The revenues of the port are quite considerable, although there are no harbour dues on ships, and this bill does not propose that such dues shall be instituted.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF BOUNDARIES AND REMUNERATION OF COMMISSIONERS OUT OF HARBOUR REVENUES
speechtext: Are there three harbour commissioners there at the present time?

subtopic: EXTENSION OF BOUNDARIES AND REMUNERATION OF COMMISSIONERS OUT OF HARBOUR REVENUES
speechtext: Yes. The late chairman, who is the appointee of the city, died recently; but the city have made a nomination to replace him and the nominee has been approved by the government, so there are three harbour commissioners. It is the practice to pay the chairman of the harbour commission of the harbour, and has been for some time, a salary as port manager. Of course it is somewhat irregular to have a member of a commission also an employee of the commission, which he is in fact under this arrangement; and instead of paying a salary of that kind to a commissioner as port manager it is proposed to pay each of the three commissioners a small salary. Perhaps the expenses of the port under this arangement will not be larger than they are at the present time.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF BOUNDARIES AND REMUNERATION OF COMMISSIONERS OUT OF HARBOUR REVENUES
speechtext: There will be no port manager appointed to replace the presumed retiring official?

subtopic: EXTENSION OF BOUNDARIES AND REMUNERATION OF COMMISSIONERS OUT OF HARBOUR REVENUES
speechtext:
I cannot say as to that.
Whether a manager will be appointed is a matter for the commission to decide. It is my understanding that it is not the intention to have a port manager appointed. However, I am not promising that for the future.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF BOUNDARIES AND REMUNERATION OF COMMISSIONERS OUT OF HARBOUR REVENUES
speechtext: This measure will not entail any additional expense as far as the Department of Transport is concerned? Revenues at the harbour will be ample to cover any additional expense which may be involved in paying additional commissioners over and above what has been paid in the past to the chief commissioner?

subtopic: EXTENSION OF BOUNDARIES AND REMUNERATION OF COMMISSIONERS OUT OF HARBOUR REVENUES
speechtext: That is correct. The Department of Transport makes no contribution whatever to harbours of that class. This property is largely owned by the city. In every instance the harbours are self-sustaining. *

subtopic: EXTENSION OF BOUNDARIES AND REMUNERATION OF COMMISSIONERS OUT OF HARBOUR REVENUES
speechtext:
Would the minister care to
comment on the principle involved in this measure, of paying harbour commissioners to look after the interests of a harbour, rather than having three commissioners on a voluntary basis, for the honour that goes with a position of that kind and the opportunity of service to their city?

subtopic: EXTENSION OF BOUNDARIES AND REMUNERATION OF COMMISSIONERS OUT OF HARBOUR REVENUES
EXTENSION OF BOUNDARIES AND REMUNERATION OF COMMISSIONERS OUT OF HARBOUR REVENUES
speechtext:
I do not know whether
I quite agree with the principle involved, be* cause to pay even a small salary for an appointment of this kind means that the position is liable to become somewhat political in its aspect, and the prey of office seekers. With each change of government some persons in New Westminster or the immediate vicinity will desire to replace these three commissioners, whereas if the commissioners were undertaking the task on a voluntary basis of service to their city you might get a higher type of person interested, and you would not be so likely to have a change, if the service had been satisfactory, with every change of government. I know there is a considerable agitation at the present time, in other harbours under the jurisdiction of the national harbours board, to have honorary commissioners under the jurisdiction of the board. The idea expressed is that these honorary officials would be particularly interested in their respective ports and in the cities which are especially connected with those ports. Here we have a departure from a principle which I think is a rather good one. I feel sure, judging by the calibre of the federal representative from New Westminster that there must be many people living in that city who would be glad of the opportunity to have this honour conferred upon them and to work in the interests of their harbour and their city.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF BOUNDARIES AND REMUNERATION OF COMMISSIONERS OUT OF HARBOUR REVENUES
speechtext: I know it.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF BOUNDARIES AND REMUNERATION OF COMMISSIONERS OUT OF HARBOUR REVENUES
speechtext:
Particularly in cooperation
and collaboration with the federal member for that district.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF BOUNDARIES AND REMUNERATION OF COMMISSIONERS OUT OF HARBOUR REVENUES
speechtext: I know it,

subtopic: EXTENSION OF BOUNDARIES AND REMUNERATION OF COMMISSIONERS OUT OF HARBOUR REVENUES
speechtext:
I believe that thereby the service would be very much improved. These men, without remuneration, would enter enthusiastically into their work; they would look at their positions from an altruistic point of view rather than from the viewpoint of the remuneration that they might receive. I am convinced that their services would be much more efficient. After all, you cannot get the type of man whom you would like to have actively interested in such a harbour as New Westminster, at the remuneration that you are prepared to pay. The compensation which may be given would not command the services of the best men available; at any rate it would not command their best service
or their full-time service. I feel that the principle involved in this proposal is one which is to be regretted. I urge upon the minister and the committee the desirability of amending this measure in such ' a way that we might at least try out for a period of time a service of commissioners who would not undertake the work for the sake of the remuneration which might be in it. I should like to hear an expression of opinion from the hon. member for New Westminster, who knows the situation better than I do. I am speaking only of the condition in general and discussing a principle. He knows the actual situation in detail. I should like him to make a statement regarding the principle involved in the bill and whether, in his opinion, the minister is correct in his presentation of it, or whether the ideas I have given voice to might not be more acceptable to the people of New Westminster than the sentiments expressed in the bill itself.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF BOUNDARIES AND REMUNERATION OF COMMISSIONERS OUT OF HARBOUR REVENUES
speechtext: I shall be pleased to do so on the second reading of the bill.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF BOUNDARIES AND REMUNERATION OF COMMISSIONERS OUT OF HARBOUR REVENUES
speechtext:
I think we have an ideal
situation at New Westminster from the point of view of my hon. friend. We have a commission made up of two Conservatives and one Liberal, all active in the pursuit of their faith. The chairman of the board is an active Conservative. In my opinion we have excellent harbour commissioners at New Westminster. I believe the progress of the port has been due largely to the attention they have given it. The commissioners themselves have urged that the change be made. They realize the anomaly of being paid more or less by subterfuge, and they think it would be better in the interests of the port for them to be paid direct and legally rather than by the present method. The city of New Westminster, which owns a large part of the port, has endorsed the opinion of the harbour commissioners, and it is the view of the government that the recommendation is one which can very well be implemented.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF BOUNDARIES AND REMUNERATION OF COMMISSIONERS OUT OF HARBOUR REVENUES
speechtext:
Has the government considered the wisdom or the feasibility of having this harbour operated, as other harbours are, under the national harbours board? That is the plan which has been adopted; it is an attractive proposal, and I do not know whether the experience of the minister would enable him to express an opinion on the advisability of having this harbour operated in that manner. We are told that it is an important harbour with a great deal of business, and possibly it might come under the jurisdiction of the national harbours board.
Xcw Westminster Harbour

subtopic: EXTENSION OF BOUNDARIES AND REMUNERATION OF COMMISSIONERS OUT OF HARBOUR REVENUES
speechtext: The position of New Westminster harbour and of a number of others, such as the harbours at Hamilton, Toronto and three or four other places that I could mention, is somewhat different from the position of the eight harbours that have been brought under the national harbours board. Whereas in the case of the eight harbours that are under the national harbours board the larger part of the investment is federal, in the case of New Westminster, Toronto and Hamilton the larger part of the investment is municipal. Under the act the municipality is entitled to representation on the board, and the funds of the harbour in excess of those required to operate or improve the port revert to the city. In the case of these harbours the city has a much larger equity than the federal government. We looked into the question when the harbour board act was passed, and consideration was given the position of these harbours. It was thought then, and I have no reason to change my opinion, that harbours of that type where the investment is largely municipal should not be brought under the board.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF BOUNDARIES AND REMUNERATION OF COMMISSIONERS OUT OF HARBOUR REVENUES
speechtext: The minister says that the investment is largely that of the city of New Westminster. I have no doubt that is correct with respect to the harbour itself, but I am sure he will agree that very substantial amounts have been expended in dredging in the Fraser river for the purpose of making conditions in the harbour satisfactory; and from time to time, I believe, that must continue. Other control works also have had to be constructed all for this purpose. It appears to me, therefore. that there is a substantial investment on the part of the dominion as well as of the city in the harbour or in something that is necessary to make the harbour a success.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF BOUNDARIES AND REMUNERATION OF COMMISSIONERS OUT OF HARBOUR REVENUES
speechtext:
I quite agree that the dominion government have spent large sums in order to make the Fraser river navigable, but I doubt whether that has any particular bearing on the administration of New Westminster harbour. Similarly, I doubt whether the fact that the federal government have spent very large sums in developing the St. Lawrence river has any particular bearing on the administration of the ports along the St. Lawrence. Fraser river is the largest river on the Pacific coast and is an important artery of traffic, and whether the port of New Westminster were there or not considerable expenditures for improving navigation on the Fraser river would be warranted. However, as I say, this port falls into the category of ports in which the city has a definite and large investment.

The city has from time to time invested considerable sums in port improvements and these sums are a charge on the taxpayers of the city. It would be considered a high-handed act for the Department of Transport to step in and take over the harbour for operation under the national harbours board.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS

speechtext:
Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Transport) moved the second reading of Bill No. 52, respecting radio in Canada.
He said: This bill repeals the present Radiotelegraph Act, revising a number of clauses therein. The necessity for changing the act at this time arises out of the fact that all paragraphs in the Radiotelegraph Act having to do with shipping have been included in the Canada Shipping Act, 1934. Therefore there is at present a duplication between the two acts. While the clauses now included in the Canada Shipping Act are being deleted from the bill, the language of the bill is being modernized. The Radiotelegraph Act was passed twenty-five years ago. Since then matters relating to communication through the ether have developed greatly; additional uses of the ether waves have been developed, and new developments in radio broadcasting have occurred for which the present act has no proper provision. The purpose then is practically the rewriting of the Radiotelegraph Act in modern language and with provisions suitable to present day conditions.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext:
Perhaps this is the proper section on which to raise a matter that relates to this bill in particular, and in general to a practice which is growing up in this house in connection with bills, and which I think should be drawn to the attention of the minister. I refer to the practice of giving in the explanatory notes information which is misleading and, in some instances, deceptive. I observe that the explanatory notes to this bill read:
The proposed bill is a revision of the Radiotelegraph Act, R.S.C. 1927, c. 195. It is revised at this time primarily because those sections referring to ships have been transferred to the Canada Shipping Act, 1934. At the same time, this has provided an opportunity to clarify and somewhat strengthen some of the remaining sections of the act, particularly with regard to the licensing of radio receiving sets used for broadcast reception.
These notes are exceedingly deceptive. The truth of the matter is that this bill introduces three new principles not previously contained in the Radiotelegraph Act so far as that act related to receiving sets and radio broadcasting. Let me outline them briefly, and as we come to them section by section I shall deal with them in detail.
In the first place this bill establishes the new principle that a radio licence collector or inspector can enter and search a man's house on a mere allegation 'by him before a magistrate that there is a radio receiving set in the possession of the occupant of that house. Under the old act it 'is true that a duly constituted and duly sworn and properly instructed police officer, a regular officer of the crown, could obtain a search warrant. But by this bill that power is extended to a radio licence collector.
The second point is that under this bill the mere possession of a radio receiving set, even though it may not be in operation, even though it has never been in operation, is made an offence. Not only is it made an offence, but it is made an indictable offence. And the indictable offence is punishable, not by the alternative of fine or imprisonment, because once one is convicted of that indictable offence the judge or magistrate must impose a fine and a penalty within the limits prescribed by the bill.
In the third place, if a person is charged with an offence under this bill, even the mere possession of a radio receiving set, and despite the fact that it is an indictable offence punishable with severe penalties as I have mentioned, the onus of proving his innocence is put upon the accused.
Those are three separate and distinct departures in principle from anything previously contained in the Radiotelegraph Act. Therefore I take this opportunity, on the very first section of this bill, of protesting against the explanatory notes given at the head thereof, and in general against explanatory notes which may be attached to amending bills in this house. It may be that I am endeavouring to set too high a standard. But I think a responsibility devolves upon a minister of the crown, when he introduces a bill in this house, to see that the explanatory notes are truly explanatory of the principles involved in the bill; and where there are radical departures from former legislation, such as there are in this bill, those departures should be clearly and distinctly drawn to the attention of the house, so that hon. members may not be misled by such notes as those which appear in this bill.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext:
The remarks of my hon. friend simply illustrate how deception can be found if a man is looking for deception. It seems to me that the explantory notes definitely call attention to the fact tha-t we are strengthening the provisions of the present act. It says:
. . . this has provided an opportunity to clarify and somewhat strengthen some of the remaining sections of the act, particularly with regard to the licensing of radio receiving sets used for broadcast reception.
How could that be made any clearer? As to providing for search, the first searches under this act were made in 1933. I remember very well my wife was almost frightened out of her life when a mounted policeman accompanied the radio inspector to our house and demanded to see her licence. I think my hon. friend was a minister of the crown at that time.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext: No; I had not that honour.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext:
Let me read the section of the old act and see if there is any material difference:
11. If a justice of the peace is satisfied by information on oath that there is reasonable ground for supposing that a radiotelegraph station has been established without a licence in that behalf, or that any apparatus for radiotelegraphy has been installed or worked in any place or on board any ship registered in Canada
Radio Broadcasting

within his jurisdiction without a licence in that behalf, he may grant a search warrant to any police officer or any officer appointed in that behalf by the minister and named in the warrant.
2. A warrant so granted shall authorize the officer named therein to enter and inspect the station, place or ship and to seize any radiotelegraph apparatus which appears to him to be there used or intended to be there used for radiotelegraphy.
I need not read the next paragraph, which provides the penalty for establishing stations and apparatus illegally. I see no great change in principle in this bill as compared with the old act, except that this bill makes it unnecessary to terrorize a house owner, as is done at the present time by a police officer in uniform marching into the premises.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext:
Let me point out the difference to the minister, if he does not see it. In the first place, under the old section it was no offence to be in possession of a radio. Let me give him the words that are added to the present section:
If a justice of the peace is satisfied by information on oath that there is reasonable ground for believing that a radio station-
Then these words are added:
-or a private receiving station has been established without a licence, or that any radio apparatus has been installed, or is being operated-
Then these words are added:
-or is in possession of any person in any place in Canada-
The minister says there is no deception. When a bill of this kind is introduced into this house, why should they not come out frankly and say in their notes what is the situation. The truth of the matter is that prosecutions were launched, and in the case of Rex v. Gignac, the citation of which I have not at the moment but which I could get if I had time to go upstairs, it was held by our courts that merely to prove that in a man's house there was a radio receiving set was not sufficient to convict that man of one of two offences, namely, that of establishing a radio station or that of operating a radio station. Because of that decision the government now proposes to amend this act to make it an offence to have in one's possession a radio receiving set, even if you never connect it and never operate it. At the moment I am not dealing with the principle of whether that should or should not be an offence.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext:
Does my hon. friend say it is deception, when the courts say that is irregular, to correct the law?
[Mr. Howe.l

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS

No; I do not say it is
deception to correct it; what.I do say is that it is deception to introduce a bill into this house and to insert a headnote stating that this is a revision of the Radiotelegraph Act, and that it is revised at this time primarily because those sections referring to ships have been transferred to the Canada Shipping Act, 1934.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext: I leave it to the members of this house whether or not, in view of the actual changes, that is a deceptive statement to insert in a headnote for the information of hon. members.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext:
Yes; it goes on to say:
At the same time, this has provided an opportunity to clarify and somewhat strengthen some of the remaining sections of the act-
It is not the intention, by this bill, somewhat to strengthen anything. The truth, of the matter is that by this bill you create a new offence, and that new offence is to merely be in possession of a radio. You not only create that offence; you create it as an indictable offence, and on top of that you do not allow any discretion to the magistrate or judge as to penalty. He must impose both a fine and imprisonment; and on top of all that you put the onus of proving his innocence upon the man who happens to be in possession of the radio receiving set. That, I say, is a deceptive explanatory note; I protest against it, and I think .the practice should be stopped.

speechtext:
I would not complain
of any specific thing if it stood alone; but let me put this to the minister. In the bills brought into the house by the Minister of Justice I have noticed that he is particularly careful to see that every change

Radio Broadcasting

is made clear to the members: he even goes to the extent, I have noticed in the bills he sponsors, of having the words that are new in each section of the amending act underlined, which calls them to the attention of the members. I ask the minister to go through this amending bill from one end to the other and find one section where the added words are underlined. I notice another thing about the bills introduced into the house by the Minister of Justice. In the explanatory notes on the right hand side he will specify the changes that are being made and the extent of them. Let me give the minister a concrete instance, though I might deal with this very section. I pick out one in particular to illustrate what I mean. Let me read the note opposite section 9 of this amending bill:
9. This is existing section 11, paragraph 1, reworded to clarify and conform to revision made in new section 5.
As a matter of fact, section 9 creates a new offence, namely, merely to be in possession of radio receiving apparatus. Let us go back to section 5. The explanatory note reads:
This is existing section 6 reworded to clarify the intention.
Whose intention? The intention of the parliament that passed the original act was determined by the courts of the land in the case of Rex v. Gignac. Why not come out frankly in this bill and say in an explanatory note. "Because the courts have held that it is not an offence merely to be in possession of a radio, this section is intended to make mere possession an offence under this act?" That gives a concrete instance of what I have in mind in the protest I am making to the Minister of Justice.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext:
I am sure we are interested in the remarks of the hon. member for York South; and in view of the curtailed explanation and statement made by the minister on the introduction of this bill, and the explanations of some of these sections that have been given by the hon. member who has just spoken, I think in a measure his comment is justified. Speaking for myself, from the statement of the minister I gathered that this was a trivial, insignificant bill; that about all it did was to rewrite the existing act because certain provisions formerly in the act may now be found in the Canada Shipping Act. But now it appears that in addition we are having a flock of new offences created, new penalties imposed and people rendered liable to proceedings and
prosecutions in a way that was not possible formerly. It seems to me that there are some grounds for the protest made by the hon. member for York South. In view of the statement of the minister I am surprised to find these provisions in the bill. In the light of the statements that have been made I am sure that we shall give the different sections careful consideration as we go along.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext:
Paragraph (e) of this section is new. This section generally empowers the governor in council to prescribe the tariff of fees to be paid for radio receiving licences, authorizes the payment of a portion of the licence fees in effect to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, authorizes the governor in council to accede to any international convention and make regulations for the censorship and controlling of radio signals. The new paragraph (e) reads:
(e) make regulations imposing a penalty not exceeding $50 and costs or three months' imprisonment for the violation of any regulation made under this section for which a penalty is not already herein prescribed, and to provide that any such penalty may be imposed upon summary conviction.
I object to this form of legislation, irrespective of whether it is in this bill or in any other bill. When you impose penalties upon the subjects, who are all the people, I think those penalties should be prescribed in the law of the land. If it is the desire of the government to have a provision imposing a penalty I suggest to the minister that he have in this bill a separate section prescribing that for any offence under it, where no other specific penalty is imposed, the penalty shall be not exceeding $50 and costs or three months' imprisonment. I suggest that the principle of fixing, by governor in council, penalties for offences is wrong under any system of responsible government. I am not criticizing this bill in particular, but I suggest that this section be taken out. If you want to have such an omnibus penalty provision, let parliament say what it is going to be and have it included as a separate section.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I referred to this matter the other day. I do not wish to criticize the minister, but I think it was a great mistake to have a debate go on such as we had the other day, and then to have to listen to the remarks of this man Ferguson
Radio Broadcasting

from Winnipeg. This gentleman and his kind are opposing the broad principles of the Chamberlain government, in relation not only to the League of Nations but to international affairs. The Prime Minister of Great Britain has ordered the British Broadcasting Corporation to stop many of these broadcasts. Just the other day I was reading criticisms of this policy in two or three eminent British papers. I have placed on Hansard just what Mr. John Buchan said with regard to this when he was a member of the British house.
These are troublesome times, but even we cannot discuss matters of this kind. It may be because the Prime Minister has been busy with other matters, but the fact is that a large number of the public hear these debates over the radio. Wrong facts or half truths are broadcast, and we hear statements absolutely opposed to the policy of the British government in connection with international agreements. I think the time has come when broadcasts of this kind should be stopped. This should be done not only in the public interest but in the interest of the British Empire.
We are prohibited from discussing questions such as Japanese immigration and the rule of Japan in the Pacific. When we as members of a free parliament start to discuss these matters points of order are raised, but the radio commission permit debates to be broadcast which are certainly objectionable to a large portion of the population of Ontario and some of the other provinces. I have read a criticism that was made in the British House of Commons of such discussions. The hon. members for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) and Essex East (Mr. Martin) spoke over the radio in a network linked up by the CBC with the NBC. I did not hear their addresses as I was on a train at the time. I read, however, with interest, their speeches on other matters.
They discussed what Mr. Cordell Hull said after the Brussels conference. What was the result of the Brussels conference? It was a failure. The British ambassador, Sir Ronald Lindsay, left his office on one side of Washington and walked a block or two to the office of the secretary of state. He asked him if the United States would join with Great Britain in making a protest to Japan, and he was told that the United States were going to act alone. All these matters come under what I describe as pan-Americanism. This broadcast was absolutely opposed to the interests of the British Empire. We are not depending upon the Monroe doctrine; we are not depending upon pan-Americanism; we are depending upon the British army, the

British navy and the British fleet to protect our shores.
What right has an outside commission to go over the heads of parliament? My right hon. leader asked if the government had been consulted at all. If we have any powers, why does the governor in council not reassert itself on behalf of this parliament and prevent these broadcasts under paragraph (d) of this section? I have no desire to criticize the commission or any official in it, but this is the view that I have taken in this house for many years. Mr. John Buchan, speaking in the British House of Commons when a member of that body, said that society consisted of the crank, the sentimentalist, and that appalling creature the publicist. Those are his words in criticizing the League of Nations Society. Two hon. members of this house and an outsider were engaged in a discussion the other day over the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation's service which was linked up with the broadcasting lines of the United States. In my opinion that broadcast should not have been allowed.
In section 3 we have the powers of the governor in council set out, and I trust that the governor in council will take the responsibility for acting in such a situation, because if we pass this section, which is a new one, the governor in council is directly responsible for what these people say in their discussions over the air. The government stopped it in England where it was held to be contrary to public policy, but anyone can go on the air through the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and enter into discussions that are not in the public interest. In the great crisis of the past six months the settled policy of the Chamberlain government has saved not only the empire, but the whole world from war.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman. I must say that I find myself very much in sympathy with the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) in the remarks which he has just made. At the present time we have been very careful not to discuss in this parliament the proceedings of other parliaments, and I believe that a rule which we find it advisable to observe here should also be observed by the commission in connection with broadcasts that may be made under its authority.
These are very critical times, as all hon. members of the house know, and as the citizens of the country generally know. In ordinary times we would not think of criticizing in this parliament the policies of a government or the proceedings of a parliament of another

Radio Broadcasting
part of the British Empire. The policies of Great Britain, of Australia and New Zealand are their own policies, their own domestic affairs, and it is not for this parliament to say whether Liberals or Conservatives or the Labour party of Great Britain are right or wrong in what they are advocating.
So far as any policy relates to our own affairs, we are at perfect liberty, of course, to discuss as fully as we please the effect of government policy. What I am referring to at the moment is not whether, with respect to some particular matter, a policy is right or wrong. Each country is free to discuss in its own parliament any policy from the point of view of that country itself. I do not think, however, that one parliament should become critical of the proceedings of another parliament in another part of the world, particularly in times like these. What applies to debates in parliament should apply equally to broadcasting under a commission which derives its authority and powers from parliament.
One of the great difficulties in Europe, a condition which make the situation there so impossible of solution, is the perpetual broadcasting by one country of its comments upon the internal affairs of some other country. I think the British government have very wisely taken the view that while they wish to accord the greatest liberty possible to broadcasting, it is not proper either in parliament or out of parliament for criticisms to be made of the internal affairs of other countries where those criticisms are likely to prove embarrassing to the government and administration of the day. I think it is only right to say what I have said; and possibly more is not necessary at this time to ensure that by the commission itself a policy will be followed similar to that which all hon. members of this house seek to follow in their discussions.
Section 3, paragraph (a) and (b) agreed to.
On section 3, paragraph (c).

speechtext: It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that a penalty of not exceeding $500 is a tremendously severe one to be left in the hands of the governor in council without reference to parliament. I may be inexperienced in these matters, but it seems a severe penalty to me.

There is no change in that
provision. It is a very serious offence to interfere with an international convention. There are on this continent only 107 channels for broadcasting purposes, which must take care of 900 existing radio stations, and it will therefore be realized that there must
be very efficient policing by each country of the channels within it. This provision is in the present Radiotelegraph Act. Those charged with administering these acts realize what a very serious offence it is to interfere with an international convention.

Paragraph agreed to.
On section 3, paragraph (d).

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext:
This seems to be
quite a paragraph. The governor in council may "make regulations for the censorship and controlling of radio signals and messages in case of actual or apprehended war, rebellion, riot or other emergency." The government is going to make regulations in respect of all these matters. What is meant by "other emergency"? What does the government consider an emergency?

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext:
This is no change from the
present legislation. Of course, to be recognized by a government as an emergency a situation must be a very, very serious one. The only change we are making here is to change the word "radiotelegraph" to "radio."

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext:
In view of certain
things which are being rumoured and the power which is here being given to the governor in council to deal with all these matters and "other emergencies," and to prescribe the punishment when the emergency is merely apprehended, it seems to me that we are conferring power upon a group of men, whoever they may be or whenever they may be acting, which will render them pretty nearly absolute dictators of the use of radio in this dominion. I personally object to that very strongly. I believe in freedom of speech. I believe in free discussion. I am completely in sympathy with the remarks of the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) and of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) with respect to not discussing matters affecting other states that may cause complications in their domestic affairs and trouble perhaps between them and us. But I think we cannot do otherwise than face the fact squarely, that there is a disposition on the part of certain people in this country to say that other people are wrong and to prevent them, whether they are right or wrong, from discussing what they have to say. This is going to lead to disaster as sure as we live, because men are going to become more and more bitter, as they are doing, and where we are going to end no one can foresee. I believe it would be quite in order for me to suggest to the minister that some change be made in the wording of this
Radio Broadcasting

paragraph so as not to leave it entirely to the governor in council to decide what the term "other emergency" shall mean.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext:
What does my hon. friend
think about the licensing of the press then?

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext: The important thing at the present time is the use of the radio; but since my hon. friend has been impertinent enough to break in with another matter not in any way connected with this, let me tell him that the "licensing of the press" made no attempt to prevent any party or group from presenting its views at as great a length as it desired. The Alberta government never attempted to limit free discussion or intended to do so. But just as sure as we are in this chamber to-night, there have been attempts made to prevent in this country free discussion of vital matters pertaining to our domestic affairs. I do not charge the minister with any wrong intention, because I have a great respect for him, and as he says, these words were in the previous act. But in the light of conditions as they are to-day we cannot be too careful. If fascism has its word to say, I should like to hear fascism express itself fully and completely over the air, so that we can all hear about it; and if communism has a case to present, let it do the same, so that the people may hear the whole story. Then, if liberalism, conservatism, the cooperative commonwealth federation and social credit have ideas which can compete successfully with those ideologies, let the people hear.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext: Shut them all off.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext:
There we have the
voice of fascism-"shut them all off!" I just wish to register my disapproval of that wording, and to urge the minister that it will be wise to specify just what is meant by it. Let me repeat that to give this body power to decide what is an emergency and what is an apprehended emergency is conferring upon them tremendous powers.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext:
This act has been on the
statute books in its present form since 1913. It was invoked only during the years of the great war, and all countries find such a provision a very necessary part of carrying on war. I think there is no possibility that the governor in council will invoke it for any minor situation.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext:
Nevertheless it places a tremendous power in the hands of the governor in council. I believe that regulations governing this question should be set out by parliament. Otherwise entirely too much power is being placed in the hands of

the governor in council, which may not be used in the best interests of large sections of the people of Canada. We know how the power has been exercised in the past by the governor in council, and that some people in this country have not been pleased with it or have not derived much satisfaction from the powers they have exercised. Now is the time parliament should assert itself and establish regulations regarding these matters, and not leave them entirely in the hands of the governor in council.

Paragraph agreed to.
On section 3, paragraph (e).

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext: I suggest to the minister that he very seriously consider, in that connection, that a penalty be prescribed not by regulation, making a separate section of the act, if he so desires, to provide that for offences for which no specific penalty' is prescribed there shall be a penalty not exceeding a fine of $50. Probably the Minister of Justice would agree with me, if he gives the matter a moment's consideration, that it is not good legislation to have penalties prescribed by the governor in council on general principle. I admit there is an exception in the case of the preceding one, covered by section 3 (d), because that is to meet an emergency condition under emergent circumstances. but this paragraph (e) is only to deal with ordinary run-of-the-mill offences which are not specifically provided for with some penalty otherwise in the act.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext:
I cannot think that the minister has read some of the speeches of his leader and of the Minister of Justice, delivered in the last parliament. If he had, I am sure he would not have presented to the house a bill containing this provision. I remember that on many occasions the present Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice very severely condemned legislation by the governor in council, and condemned it when it did not occupy the field of imposing penalties, and they were particularly severe whenever it was suggested that the governor in council might impose a penalty. I cannot believe that the Minister of Justice saw this section before it was presented to the committee. Certainly it is in direct opposition to the position his party have taken during a period of four or five years in connection with similar sections in other legislation. The position taken by the hon. member for York South is absolutely sound. A penalty of this kind ought to be found in a section of the act, and it ought not to be left to the discretion or to the judgment of the governor

Radio Broadcasting
iu council to impose penalties. We should know, when a penalty is being imposed, what it is, the extent of it and what it is for, why the penalty is imposed. I call attention to the fact that this is a new section; that it is not found in the act. The minister cannot justify it on that ground. He is inserting a new section which, as I have said, is contrary to the position that was taken and adhered to and reiterated and emphasized by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice in the years gone by. I am sure the Minister of Justice will agree with me that on former occasions he has taken the position which I am now taking.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS

As regards this clause 3, paragraph (e), inasmuch as I had to disagree with the hon. member for York South this afternoon, I am very glad at this time to say that I agree with him. I do not think we should give the governor in council the power to make regulations to impose penalties. To my mind it is just as easy to insert the provision in a section of the act. For instance it could be subsection 2, reading as follows:
Any person convicted of a violation of any of the regulations made under this section for which a penalty is not already herein prescribed shall be liable upon summary conviction to a penalty not exceeding fifty dollars and costs or three months' imprisonment.
It would be just as easy to have it in a section of the act as to make it subject to regulation by order in council.

Now I find that the governor in council can impose a penalty, and they are given absolute control. Parliament is given no right to say what the penalty shall be or what the regulation shall be.

speechtext:
In this discussion as to licences and penalties, I wonder whether the minister would think it unreasonable if I asked him to inform the committee the government's attitude in connection with radio patents. I fully realize that patents come under another department, but at the same time it is up to the minister to initiate any action for the relief of the public. For instance, let us take an example such as this: A man purchases a radio and pays his licence fee of $2.50. It just so happens that he bought that radio in the United States- why? Because the action of Radio Patents Limited permit the radio manufacturers in Canada, about twelve in number, to charge anywhere from 50 to 100 per cent more for the same style of radio produced in Canada than is charged in the United States. That man has paid his licence fee and along comes Radio Patents Limited and asserts its right, as it contends, to confiscate that radio and destroy it. It makes the purchaser sign an undertaking that he will not bring a radio into Canada; that he will not use one; that he will not sell one, or manufacture one. That situation is created entirely by a series of patents held by a holding company, and these manufacturers lease from that holding company the privilege of using their own patents. And, of course, the royalty they pay is tacked on to the cost of the Canadian-made radio.
We know that the matter is before the tariff board, 'but in the meantime the government is in full possession of the facts. It knows that these people will assert their right, so-called, to confiscate a man's radio. The government knows that the purchase price in Canada is anywhere from 50 to 100 per cent in excess of the price in the United States. In view of these facts, does the minister not think that, without waiting for action on the part of the tariff board some action should be taken at once to relieve the public of these impositions made by Radio Patents Limited?

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext:
I think the government has taken the logical step in ordering a full investigation of the situation. The situation has been known for many years and there has been a growing realization of it. It is, of course, a complicated matter. Our patent
Radio Broadcasting

Jaws are there, and it is our own patent laws that make the situation possible. Bringing out the full facts and disclosing all sides of the question is a necessary step before any action can be taken.

I was of the opinion that this was an exaggeration; but even if it is, that point should be definitely established. I understood the minister to say that the matter was before the tariff board for a ruling. Has there been a ruling on it?
