subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext:
Action could be taken under the combines act. It does seem unreasonable for the public to have to continue suffering under these impositions. Under section 11 of the combines act immediate action could be taken to remedy the situation. It is almost incredible that a Canadian citizen cannot purchase a radio in the United States, bring it into Canada after he has paid the duty, and enjoy the possession of it, but that is the fact. He cannot bring a radio in from any country even though he pays the fully assessed duty and the sales and excise tax. He simply cannot bring it in and call it his own. Just ihink of any corporation having the power to confiscate a man's radio after he has paid for it and paid the government duty and obtained his licence, while the government does not interfere but is simply willing to wait for the tariff board to investigate the matter, though we know that this condition exists. We have already put the facts on Hansard; we have stated cases. There is the case of the Winnipeg concern where they were permitted to sell their radios on condition that they paid a royalty and all legal charges. We had cases in Prince Rupert. There was a case in my own home town. A man simply refused to sign the undertaking, and he was told that if it occurred again Radio Patents Limited would exercise its right to confiscate his radio and destroy it, a radio that he had paid for and brought in. It is true he brought it in under the $100 exemption, tout he declared it and got his clearance. It makes no difference,

however, whether you bring it in under the $100 exemption, or in the regular course, paying the customs duty; Radio Patents Limited still asserts its right to confiscate your radio and destroy it. Let me ask the minister this question: Is there any reason under the sun why that state of affairs should continue? Should there not be more speedy action than is possible as a result of a mere reference to the tariff board? Is the matter going to drag for another year? I know just about how much has been paid in royalty by these radio manufacturers to Radio Patents Limited for the privilege of using their own patents, and then that royalty is tacked on to the price of the Canadian-made radio. Does the minister not think that there should be more immediate action than we can obtain by waiting for the outcome of a long drawn out hearing by the tariff board? The combines act would permit of such action, and the public would feel much better disposed towards the department and the radio business in general if such action were taken.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext:
Perhaps a word as to
the manner in which the present reference to the tariff board originated might be useful at this stage. Representations were made to the government last year regarding unreasonably high prices, particularly of radio products. Allegations were made that these outrageous prices were probably made possible by the operation of the tariff. Other statements were made similar to those just made by the hon. member, and denials and qualifications and all the rest of it came in great volume from those affected. The government determined that I should make a reference to the tariff board with respect to the bearing of tariffs on the conditions revealed in the radio industry. But in examining the matter for the purpose of reference it did not take me long to come to the conclusion that such an investigation could not lead to anything of value unless it included a full investigation of the manner in which the Canadian patent law operates with respect to radio. I would point out that the patent law operates with respect to any commodity coming within its provisions; there is no difference in the treatment of radio or radio tubes and parts and the treatment of any other commodity under that law. But because of the circumstances to which my hon. friend referred I believed that no investigation by the tariff board could produce useful results unless there were combined in the reference the investigation of the manner in which the patent law operates in connection with the price structure and prices charged and the provisions of sale of radio parts. For that reason this method

Radio Broadcasting
was chosen as being the one most likely to bring out the facts of the situation both from the standpoint mentioned by the hon. member and with respect to the bearing of the tariff on the cost of radios and radio parts.
I	expect that the tariff board will be proceeding very shortly with the hearing, which I can assure my hon. friend will be a very thorough investigation into the whole matter. I think we have at our disposal no more effective machinery for investigating the whole matter. An investigation dealing only with the patent law would be subject to two difficulties: (1) that the patent law is the same with respect to any article which is patented, and any abuse which exists may not be confined to radio but possibly extend to other patented articles; (2) an investigation based only on patent law would ignore the tariff aspects of the problem. So for that reason it was thought well to hive an investigation before a body competent to go into all aspects of the matter and to give to parliament and the country the facts upon which judgment could be intelligently based. There are many views on the matter. Personally I am inclined to the view expressed by the hon. member, but certainly that view is contradicted very strongly by those interested in the business. By the means we have adopted we shall be sure of a complete understanding of the facts. The tariff board can call to its assistance auditors and experts of any kind, go right into the business of the people concerned and get all the facts.

If our law is weak in that respect, I should like to see the gap closed by this parliament.

licence fees for broadcasting companies would come under this section. The question I want to bring to the attention of the minister relates to some confusion which seems to exist. A small station in my district, each time it applied for a licence in the last five years, applied for increase of power from 100 to 250. I discussed the matter with the manager of the broadcasting corporation a couple of days ago and he promised to go into it thoroughly. But there appears to be considerable confusion.
